docs.title: IPU Emulator Documentation
docs.text:
The IPU (Inference Processing Unit) is a 128-lane VLIW vector processor for neural-network inference. This repository defines its instruction set, assembles programs for it, emulates it in Python, and holds the kernels that run on it. Bazel builds and tests everything.

Section Go here to Getting started Install the toolchain, run the tests and run a first kernel. How-to Write, register or debug a kernel, or add an instruction. Reference Look up an instruction, an operand type, a command, a kernel or a term. Explanation Understand the architecture, the timing model and the element formats. Specs and requirements Read the hardware block specifications and requirements. Open questions See every open hardware, emulator and ISA question. Release log See what changed in each merged pull request.

The source is on GitHub. README.md has the Quick Start.

docs.title: Explanation
docs.text:
These pages are for understanding how the IPU and its tools work and why they are built this way.

Page What it covers Architecture The packages, how they depend on each other, how a program goes from source to a checked run, and prototyping mode. Timing model Which register values each stage reads within a cycle. Element formats Each element format, how it encodes values, how a CR scalar is decoded in it, and how a kernel selects one. ISA idioms The instruction sequences kernels use for operations the ISA lacks, why, and what each costs. Kernel coverage How a computation resolves to a kernel, and which operations the kernels cover.

The architecture decision records in docs/adr/ record the decisions behind the design.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: The toolchain is seven Python packages under src/, one directory each. Each package has one responsibility, and dependencies point one way: towards ipu_isa, the instruction set, which imports no other package. Terms such as instruction word, slot, commit record and harness are defined in the glossary; the decisions behind the design are the architecture decision records in docs/adr/; the rules for writing code in these packages are the code conventions.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
An arrow points from a package to a package it imports. The diagram leaves out an arrow that another path already implies: ipu_harness imports ipu_isa directly, and the path through ipu_as stands for it.

flowchart TD
    ipu_isa[ipu_isa]
    ipu_as[ipu_as]
    ipu_emu[ipu_emu]
    ipu_debug[ipu_debug]
    ipu_gen[ipu_gen]
    ipu_harness[ipu_harness]
    ipu_kernels[ipu_kernels]
    ipu_as --> ipu_isa
    ipu_emu --> ipu_isa
    ipu_debug --> ipu_emu
    ipu_gen --> ipu_as
    ipu_harness --> ipu_as
    ipu_harness --> ipu_debug
    ipu_kernels --> ipu_harness
Package Directory What it owns Imports Imported by ipu_isa src/ipu-isa/ The IPU instruction set, the single source of truth: instructions, slots, operand types, registers, element formats, the timing contract and the binary codec. nothing ipu_as, ipu_debug, ipu_emu, ipu_gen, ipu_harness, ipu_kernels ipu_as src/ipu-as/ The assembler: assembly source, optionally a Jinja2 template, to instruction words. ipu_isa ipu_gen, ipu_harness ipu_emu src/ipu-emu/ The IPU cycle-functional emulator: machine state, the cycle module, per-slot handlers, prototyping mode and the stable reference-model API (ipu_emu.reference). ipu_isa ipu_debug, ipu_harness ipu_debug src/ipu-debug/ The IPU emulator's interactive debugger: a curses TUI (ipu_debug.tui) over ipu_emu.emulator.run_with_debug. ipu_emu, ipu_isa ipu_harness ipu_gen src/ipu-gen/ Generators that render artifacts from the ISA (ipu_isa): the SystemVerilog package, the generated docs pages and the VS Code language data. ipu_as, ipu_isa nothing ipu_harness src/ipu-harness/ The kernel framework: everything between a kernel's declaration and a checked run. ipu_as, ipu_debug, ipu_emu, ipu_isa ipu_kernels ipu_kernels src/ipu-kernels/ Kernel-side Python shared across kernels: references, pack transforms, family code. ipu_harness, ipu_isa nothing
  • ipu_kernels.reference may import only ipu_isa.
  • ipu_harness imports torch only inside a function.

The diagram and the table are generated at docs build time (docs/architecture_page.py) from tools/import_graph.toml and the first paragraph of each package's __init__.py docstring. A renamed or added package changes this page with no doc edit.

tools/import_graph.toml is the one list of allowed edges. //tools:test_import_graph reads every source of every package and fails on a first-party import its package's row does not list, including an import inside a function. Each package's Bazel deps enforce the same edges at build time: an import outside them fails in the sandbox.

Two edges are absent by design. Nothing imports ipu_gen: it reads the ISA and the assembler's parser and writes files. ipu_harness never imports ipu_kernels: the registry, pack and reference lookups load kernel-side modules by a name read from registry data, as plugins.

docs.title: One source of truth
docs.text:
src/ipu-isa/src/ipu_isa/instruction_spec.py defines every instruction: its slot, operands, timing declaration, documentation and handler name. An instruction's opcode is its position in its slot's table, never a number written by hand. Every other package reads the ISA through the typed view ipu_isa.view.isa(); only ipu_isa's loader reads the authoring tables (ADR 0001).

Derived artifact Built by From the ISA it takes Word layout, slot codec, disassembly ipu_isa.codec Field widths, opcodes, operand types Assembler grammar and encoder ipu_as Mnemonics, operand names and types Emulator dispatch ipu_emu (plans_for in ipu.py) One plan per opcode: its execute_<name> handler, operand fields, register reads and fault checks SystemVerilog package ipu_gen.sv_package The word layout and every *_WIDTH ISA reference pages and layout SVGs ipu_gen.docs_pages, ipu_gen.layout_svg Instruction docs, operand types, registers VS Code language data ipu_gen.vscode_data Mnemonics and register names

The "one edit" test proves it. It adds a dummy instruction, TESTNEG, as one spec entry and one handler, and checks that every artifact follows: //src/ipu-isa:test_one_edit for the ISA's own artifacts, src/ipu-gen/test/test_one_edit_generators.py for the generators, and src/ipu-emu/test/test_one_edit_end_to_end.py for an assembled program running on the emulator. Its list of manual edits beyond the entry and the handler, KNOWN_MANUAL_EDITS, is empty. How-to: add an instruction walks through the same edit.

docs.title: Life of a program
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    src[".asm source"] --> session["AssemblySession<br/>(ipu_as)"]
    session --> codec["word codec<br/>(ipu_isa.codec)"]
    codec --> load["load_program<br/>(ipu_emu.reference)"]
    load --> cycle["Cycle: one word<br/>(ipu_emu.cycle)"]
    cycle --> record["commit record"]
    record --> compare["compare with golden<br/>(ipu_harness)"]
  1. Assemble. ipu_as.session.AssemblySession renders the source's Jinja2 layer once, parses it, resolves labels and encodes each instruction word. Every failure is an AssemblerError with a source location.
  2. Encode. The word codec in ipu_isa.codec.word packs the words into a program file. The emulator decodes with the same codec, so the assembler and the emulator never hold two copies of the layout.
  3. Load. ReferenceModel.load_program (ipu_emu.reference) writes the words into instruction memory. The harness also writes the inputs to XMEM and sets the CRs its ABI names.
  4. Plan the word. At each pc, schedule_word (ipu_emu.cycle) turns the word into a Schedule: the issued instruction of each slot, in slot execution order, with any F-1 or F-3 fault found before a slot runs. The schedule is a pure function of the word, so it is built once per pc and cached until that instruction memory entry is written.
  5. Run one cycle. Cycle (ipu_emu.cycle) is the one module that executes an instruction word. It takes the cycle-start register values, evaluates BREAK, runs the LR sub-slots and every other slot in order, and runs the fault checks after the LR slot. Each slot's instruction runs through its handler in ipu_emu.slots (execute_<name>, keyword arguments named after the spec's operands). A handler reads registers through CycleView, which returns the cycle-start or the forwarded value as the timing contract declares.
  6. Commit. The word retires as a commit record: the pc before and after, the instruction retired in each slot, the register and XMEM writes, and any halt or fault. ReferenceModel.step returns it; run writes each one to a trace when given a TraceWriter.
  7. Compare. The harness (ipu_harness.runner.run_kernel) runs the program to HALT, reads the output regions back from XMEM, unpacks them, and compares each with its golden at the kernel's tolerance tier (ipu_harness.compare). A faulting run returns its fault instead of a comparison.

docs.title: Faithful and prototyping execution
docs.text:
By default the emulator models what the hardware does, slot by slot: every slot is dispatched even when it holds a NOP, every multiply applies its element mask, and every cycle reads the full cycle-start register values. That fidelity is what makes the emulator answerable about the chip.

Prototyping mode trades some of it for speed on long runs, where the question is "what does this kernel compute" rather than "what does the chip do". It is an adapter over the faithful path, not a second emulator: the same Cycle runs both, and prototyping mode changes four things on it, all listed in ipu_emu.prototyping.

Shortcut Why it is safe Why it is not faithful Schedules leave out slots holding an idle NOP (skip_idle_nops) Their handlers do nothing The machine still issues the slot Read operands go through the packed resolver (ipu_emu.resolver.PackedResolver) The values and invalid-index exceptions match the generated accessors It bypasses the normal register-access machinery A MULT with no mask shift and an all-ones mask skips the mask pipeline It deactivates no lane, so MULT_RES is unchanged The mask is applied on every multiply in hardware A full-row FP32 ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE without output quantization runs as one batched row It keeps the scalar arithmetic, the FP32 store boundary, exceptions and partial writes The hardware activation pipeline works lane by lane

The cond slot's NOP is never skipped, because execute_cond_nop advances the pc.

docs.title: What it guarantees
docs.text:
The state after every cycle is bit-identical to the faithful path: every register, all of XMEM, the cycle count and the run statistics. src/ipu-emu/test/test_prototyping_equivalence.py runs each program in lockstep, once per mode, and compares every register, all 512 MiB of XMEM, cycle outcomes, the cycle-start register values and run statistics after every cycle. It also runs every register-timing probe (src/ipu-emu/test/timing_probes.py, one minimal program per row of the timing tables) in every element format the probe covers.

At kernel level, each case's baseline record (baseline.json beside each kernel's test.py) is recorded in a default build and checked unchanged in a flagged one. Each case's program, setup, output, final state and cycle count must be identical in both modes.

Prototyping mode does not guarantee that the work the emulator did resembles the work the chip would do. Trust the numbers a prototyping run produces; do not reason from it about what a cycle costs the hardware.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
bazel test --config=proto //...

--config=proto (.bazelrc) is the short form of --define=ipu_proto=1. The Bazel flag is mandatory: a default build and a plain checkout cannot activate the shortcuts, and requesting them there raises ValueError.

Level How Use Build gate --config=proto (--define=ipu_proto=1) Required; prototyping mode is the default in that build Per state IpuState(prototyping=True/False) Select a mode inside a flagged build Per process IPU_EMU_PROTOTYPING=1/0 Select the default inside a flagged build

IPU_EMU_PROTOTYPING is read case-insensitively, with surrounding whitespace ignored. 0, false, no, off and the empty string mean off, in any build. 1, true, yes and on mean on. Any other value raises ValueError.

CI runs the default tier in both modes on every pull request. The proto job fails if any case of test_prototyping_equivalence is skipped. The nightly workflow runs the heavy tier with the flag too.

docs.title: What it is worth
docs.text:
The representative workload is FP32 softmax_rows with 128 rows. Assembly and input preparation are outside the timed region. Each version received two independent warm-ups followed by 14 measured runs in total:

Version Median time Throughput Gain vs master master (ea7613e) 0.7197 s 3,228 cycles/s baseline performance-fix (b072bb3) 0.1145 s 20,280 cycles/s 6.28x Prototyping mode 0.07118 s 32,636 cycles/s 10.11x

That is 1.61x over performance-fix, or 37.9% less wall time. All versions executed 2,323 cycles and produced the same output SHA-256:

16c5777b09191f41d5f965097b0a29372cb42eb1d608d1450045989bcd6549ae

These figures describe one machine and workload, not a universal speedup. Kernels with partial activation rows or other activation functions take the scalar activation path; other instruction mixes gain in other proportions.

docs.title: Stable and internal code
docs.text: Only the reference model API is stable: the names of ipu_emu.reference, the commit records its step() returns and the commit record and trace schemas. The Reference model API page lists them and says what a breaking change is. Everything else in ipu_emu, and every other package's Python API, is internal and can change in any release (ADR 0004). The harness drives the emulator through the reference model API only, like an RTL testbench.

docs.title: Element formats
docs.text: An element format says how the IPU reads the elements of a vector: how many bits each element has and what number those bits stand for. A run is in one of two modes, chosen when it starts, and each mode has one element format: NX8, the hardware's, and FP32, the emulator's. The program is the same in both modes; the mode decides what its loads, multiplies and stores compute (ADR 0007).

docs.title: The formats
docs.text:
Format Tag Element bits Metadata bits Row bytes Accumulator FP32 EMULATOR 32 0 512 FP32 NX8 HARDWARE 8 16 128 FP32

The table is generated from ipu_isa.formats.

  • Row bytes. An XMEM row holds one element per lane, 128 elements, and every load and store moves exactly one row: 128 bytes and a 16-bit metadata word in NX8, 512 bytes in FP32. LD.MASK and LD.LUT read the first 128 bytes of a row in both modes.
  • Accumulator type. MULT_RES and R_ACC hold FP32 in both modes: in NX8 the multiplier expands each element to FP32 first.
  • Register element widths. R0, R1 and R_CYCLIC hold one row's elements per register (or R_CYCLIC slot), and in NX8 the row's metadata word beside them; R_MASK is the same in both modes.

NX8 (hardware). The IPU's only element format: 8-bit elements whose meaning depends on a per-row scale and on a QF (quantization format), a 16-bit half of a CR that each instruction names. It is a family of types, not one format: the QF chooses the type of every vector an instruction reads or writes.

FP32 (emulator only). IEEE float32 elements, with no metadata, no scaling and no quantization; every QF operand is ignored. It runs a kernel written for NX8 at full precision, so its result can be compared with a reference such as PyTorch. The assembly and its XMEM row numbers are the same as in NX8; each element takes four bytes instead of one.

FP32 and NX8 are the only element formats. "E4" means the NX8 type e4.

docs.title: How NX8 encodes values
docs.text:
An NX8 type comes from a QF half (Configuration registers): num_bits W (1–8), exp_format fe (1–7), sign (0 or 1) and dynamic. An element has sign sign bits, fe exponent bits and fm = W − fe − sign mantissa bits, in the top W bits of its byte.

A row's 16-bit metadata word holds scale[7:0] (an e8m0 exponent, bias 127) and dynamic_exponent[8]. The element's exponent field is a distance below the scale, so one byte means different values in different rows:

  • An exponent field e below all ones is normal: (1 + m / 2fm) × 2scale − 127 − e.
  • The all-ones exponent field is the subnormal range: (m / 2fm) × 2scale − 127 − (2fe − 2); with mantissa 0 it is zero.
  • There is no NaN and no infinity (OQ-37).

Dynamic types are signed and 8 bits wide; each row chooses fe = 1 or 2 (dynamic_exponent 0 or 1 in its metadata) by the architecture spec's rule (ARCH-stage-aaq-str.md §4.3.2.3), with errors measured in units of the row's scale (OQ-49).

The values each fixed type holds at unit scale (scale 127), computed from the codec (ipu_isa.nx8.decode_element):

Type Exponent bits Mantissa bits Largest Smallest normal Smallest nonzero E1 1 6 1.984375 1 0.015625 E2 2 5 1.96875 0.25 0.0078125 E3 3 4 1.9375 0.015625 0.0009765625 E4 4 3 1.875 2-14 2-17 E5 5 2 1.75 2-30 2-32 E6 6 1 1.5 2-62 2-63 E7 7 0 1 2-126 2-126

Quantizing a row (ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE, ipu_isa.nx8.encode_row):

  • Scale. The row's scale is the largest FP32 exponent among its active finite elements. FP32 inputs are always treated as normalized, so an all-zero row gets scale 0 and reads back as 2-127 (open questions).
  • Rounding. Each element rounds to the nearest value; a tie rounds up.
  • Saturation. ±inf saturates to the largest magnitude and is left out of the scale; a negative input to an unsigned type encodes as 0. Each sets the QUANT_SATURATION arithmetic event.
  • NaN. A NaN to quantize is an emulator error: NX8 cannot hold it.
  • Inactive elements (outside the DS half's active elements) are written as 0 (OQ-36).

Expanding an element for a multiply is the inverse: the MULT decodes each element with the QF half it names and the metadata of the row the element was loaded from (ARCH-stage-mult.md §3.2.1). LD.MULT and LD.MULT.CYCLIC copy that metadata into R0, R1 or the R_CYCLIC slot.

XMEM keeps the metadata in a side store, one word per 128-byte unit. Metadata that was never written reads 0, like unwritten data.

docs.title: CR scalars
docs.text:
A CR holds 32 bits. MULT.VE, MULT.EE and MULT.RC.VE (with a CR as src) use a CR as a scalar element, a MULT constant: they multiply a vector by it.

Format CR bits Decoded as FP32 [31:0] an IEEE binary32 value; CR0 is 0.0 and CR1 1.0 NX8 [23:0] (bits 31:24 ignored) one NX8 element with its own scale and type (the constant layout); CR0 is 0.0 and CR1 1.0

In NX8 the constant is one element with its own scale and type, independent of the vector's QF: value[7:0], scale[15:8], fe[19:16] and sign[23:20], always 8 bits wide and never dynamic (ipu_isa.cr_halves.constant). In FP32 it is the float32 bit pattern. CR0 and CR1 are the exceptions: as MULT constants they read as 0.0 and 1.0 in both modes, so a multiply by CR1 is an identity multiply whatever the mode.

This program multiplies a vector of ones by CR3, so every element of MULT_RES is the scalar as the mode decodes it:

# Ra (R0 ++ R1) holds 1.0 in every element, so each MULT_RES element is the decoded scalar.
# CR15.L is the DS (every element active), CR14.L the QF of the vectors (NX8 e4).
PROGRAM = """
MULT.VE LR0 CR3 0 LR2 CR15.L CR14.L;;
HALT;;
"""
CR3 = {
    # The MULT constant layout: the e4 element 0x08 (0.5) under scale 2^3.
    ElementFormat.NX8: constant(value=0x08, scale=SCALE_BIAS + 3, exp_format=4),
    # The float32 bit pattern of 1.0 (0x3F800000) plus 0x38.
    ElementFormat.FP32: 0x3F80_0038,
}

The test that runs it checks element 0 of MULT_RES in each mode:

EXPECTED = {
    ElementFormat.NX8: 4.0,  # exponent 1 below the scale: 2^-1, times 2^3
    ElementFormat.FP32: 1 + 56 * 2**-23,  # all 32 bits as a float32: 1.0 plus 56 ulps
}

docs.title: Selecting a mode
docs.text:
The mode is emulator configuration, not a CR value. Choose it when you construct the state, or reset the state into the other mode:

from ipu_emu.ipu_state import IpuState
from ipu_isa.formats import ElementFormat

state = IpuState(fmt=ElementFormat.NX8)  # the default

# Or return an existing state to reset, in the other mode.
state.reset(ElementFormat.FP32)

state.fmt cannot be assigned. An unknown format raises ConfigurationError when the state is built, never while a program runs.

A kernel lists its variants in its kernel.toml's [kernel] formats: fp32 for the FP32 mode, and for NX8 a named type (e1 to e7, dynamic) or s<sign>e<fe>w<bits>. A case can list a subset in its own formats; otherwise it runs in each of the kernel's variants. The harness binds the case's QF where the kernel asks for it (case_qf).

docs.title: XMEM layout per mode
docs.text:
An XMEM operand in assembly (offset + base) is a row number in both modes. A row is 128 elements, so its width depends on the mode: row r starts at byte r × 128 in NX8 and r × 512 in FP32. A program reaches the same row in both modes. NX8 addresses only the first 16384 rows of XMEM.

  • LD.MULT reads one row (128 elements, and its metadata) into R0 or R1.
  • LD.MULT.CYCLIC reads one row into one of the four slots of R_CYCLIC. Its index must be a slot boundary: 0, 128, 256 or 384.
  • ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE stores one row: 128 NX8 bytes and the row's metadata, or 128 FP32 values. ACTIVATE.EXACT (FP32 only) stores one FP32 row.
  • Register indices count elements. rc_idx, ra_idx and the cyclic index are element indices in both modes.
  • Element data in XMEM is little-endian float32 in FP32 and one byte per element in NX8.

The kernel harness packs each tensor for the case's variant (ipu_harness.packing): in NX8 it quantizes each row and writes its metadata, and reads both back for an output.

docs.title: How FP32 computes
docs.text:
• Multiply and accumulate. IEEE float arithmetic, in both modes once the NX8 elements are expanded.
  • Masks. The mask-and-shift on MULT_RES is the same in both modes: each of the 128 mask bits gates one element.
  • Stores. ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE stores the activated FP32 row without quantizing it; ACTIVATE.EXACT applies the exact activation instead of the hardware list (ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE, ACTIVATE.EXACT and LD.LUT).

docs.title: Arithmetic events
docs.text: An accumulator overflow or a NaN result is an arithmetic event, not a fault: see Arithmetic events. What the emulator does on an FP32 overflow is OQ-18 in Open questions.

docs.title: ISA idioms
docs.text:
The IPU instruction set has no vector move, add, subtract or broadcast. Kernels build each missing operation from a short sequence of instructions it does have. This page lists each sequence (an idiom, numbered A1 to A15), why the ISA forces it, and what it costs.

Most idioms trace to one fact: every ACC.* and AGG.* instruction consumes MULT_RES. Every path into the accumulator crosses the multiplier, and the MULT slot has no move, add, subtract or pass-through form. A multiply by a constant 1.0 therefore stands in for all of them. It occupies the multiplier for a cycle without doing arithmetic.

In the examples, CR1 is the MULT constant 1.0 (in both modes), CR15.L holds the DS (data structure) half and CR14.L the QF (quantization format) half the NX8 elements are decoded with (Configuration registers). ; separates the slots of one instruction word and ;; ends the word.

Every run counts how often each idiom occurred. To measure them in a kernel, see The kernel is too slow in the debug how-to; the options are in the command-line reference.

docs.title: A1 — MOV.RC: move a vector into the accumulator
docs.text:
A multiply by 1.0 followed by ACC.ADD.FIRST copies a vector into R_ACC. Every other identity-multiply idiom on this page is a special case of this one.

# Form 1 - R_CYCLIC vector x CR one
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # R_CYCLIC <- source, one word ahead
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0, routing only
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;                # ACC.ADD accumulates instead

# Form 2 - R_CYCLIC x an all-ones row resident in R0
    LD.MULT R0 LR2 CR2 ;;           # R0 <- 128 x 1.0, loaded once
    MULT.RC.VV LR0 R0 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;

# Form 3 - one element, broadcast to all 128 lanes
    MULT.EE LR1 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;

MULT.VE is the form for a source already in R0 or R1. Form 2 also takes an R0/R1 register and an XMEM row for the ones vector.

docs.title: A2 — ADD.VV / ADD.VS: vector add
docs.text:
Each addend passes through the multiplier against 1.0, and the accumulator sums them.

# Form 1 - vector + vector (residual add): two passes, one accumulator
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # R_CYCLIC <- A
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # A x 1.0
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # R_CYCLIC <- B, in the same word
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # B x 1.0
    ACC.ADD ;;

# Form 2 - vector + scalar
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # vector x 1.0
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;
    MULT.EE LR1 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;    # scalar broadcast x 1.0
    ACC.ADD ;;

docs.title: A3 — SUB.VV / NEG: vector subtract and negate
docs.text:
ACC.SUB exists, but its operand still comes from MULT_RES, so the subtrahend passes through the multiplier first.

# Subtract: stage the subtrahend, subtract in the ACC slot
    MULT.EE LR1 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;    # broadcast x 1.0
    ACC.SUB ;;                      # for example softmax's x - max

# Negate, into an empty accumulator
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0
    ACC.SUB.FIRST ;;                # R_ACC = -MULT_RES

A multiply by a CR that holds -1.0 costs the same: the sign moves from the ACC slot to the multiplier.

docs.title: A4 — AGG.SUM.RC / AGG.MAX.RC: reduce a register
docs.text:
A reduction reads only MULT_RES, never a vector register.

    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0
    AGG.SUM.FIRST LR3 CR15.L ;;     # AGG.SUM accumulates across words
    # AGG.MAX.FIRST reduces to the maximum; ACC.MAX keeps an elementwise running maximum

AGG.* reduces lanes 0 .. valid_elements-1 of its DS half to the one slot LR[LR3] % 128.

docs.title: A5 — BCAST / SPLAT: replicate one value across lanes
docs.text:
MULT.EE is the only broadcast path, so a broadcast costs a multiply.

# Form 1 - one Ra element -> all 128 lanes
    MULT.EE LR1 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;    # x 1.0
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;

# Form 2 - windowed broadcast: one partition-sized window -> every partition.
# One pass per partition p: rc_idx = (-partition_size * p) mod 512 selects the
# read window, mask_offset = p the write window. This is the pass for p = 1.
    SET LR4 CR3 ;;                  # CR3 = (-partition_size * p) mod 512
    MULT.RC.VE LR4 CR1 1 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # mask_offset = p = 1
    ACC.ADD ;;

# Form 3 - ACC.RESHAPE: 8 lanes per instruction, still behind the multiplier
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0
    ACC.RESHAPE LRD0 LRD2 0 ;;      # MULT_RES[src[i]] -> R_ACC[dst[i]]

Form 2 costs one multiply per partition. Form 3 reads 8 elements of an LRDn pair as source and destination lane indices, so a 16-lane partition takes two ACC.RESHAPE instructions, each after an identity multiply that fills MULT_RES.

docs.title: A6 — GATHER / SCATTER / PERMUTE / ROTATE
docs.text:
A masked multiply by 1.0 moves lanes: rc_idx selects the read window and mask_offset the write window.

# Form 1 - gather or scatter
    MULT.RC.VE LR4 CR1 3 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0, write window 3
    ACC.ADD ;;

# Form 2 - rotate across lanes. R_CYCLIC does not wrap at 128, so the row is
# loaded twice, back to back, and read at a shifted offset.
    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR2 ;; # drain R_ACC to scratch
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # copy 1 at R_CYCLIC offset 0
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR5 ;;   # copy 2 at R_CYCLIC offset 128
    MULT.RC.VE LR6 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # LR6 = rotate amount
    ACC.MAX ;;

# Form 3 - ACC.RESHAPE: any 8-lane permutation, MULT_RES -> R_ACC
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0
    ACC.RESHAPE LRD0 LRD2 0 ;;

docs.title: A7 — REDUCE.SEG: reduce each partition
docs.text:
Every AGG.* instruction produces one scalar, so N partition sums take N passes.

# Drain the 128 lanes that hold N partitions of partition_size
    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR2 ;;
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # reload into R_CYCLIC

# One pass per partition p, at rc_idx = partition_size * p
    SET LR4 CR3 ;;                  # CR3 = partition_size * 0
    MULT.RC.VE LR4 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;
    SET LR4 CR4 ;;                  # CR4 = partition_size * 1
    MULT.RC.VE LR4 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # x 1.0
    ACC.ADD ;;
    # and so on, to p = N-1

The DS half's num_partitions encodes the grouping, but it feeds only the mask-shift arithmetic; it moves and reduces no data.

docs.title: A8 — MOV.ACC: return R_ACC to the multiply stage
docs.text:
R_ACC has no path back to the multiply-stage inputs. The value goes out to XMEM and back in.

# Drain: identity is a move, no activation
    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR2 ;;

# Reload, into either input
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # -> R_CYCLIC
    LD.MULT R0 LR2 CR2 ;;           # -> R0 / R1

The move needs no identity multiply. It costs one xmem_write, one xmem_read and the round-trip latency. In the NX8 mode it also quantizes the row to the QF half's NX8 format on the way out (with a scale of its own in the row's metadata), so it is a lossy move. In the FP32 mode ACTIVATE.EXACT identity CR15.L CR2 LR2 moves the FP32 row unchanged.

docs.title: A9 — EXP: only exp2 exists
docs.text:
The activation unit has exp2. A kernel computes exp(x) as exp2(x * log2(e)).

    LD.MULT R0 LR2 CR2 ;;           # R0 <- 128 x log2(e), loaded once
    MULT.RC.VV LR0 R0 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;  # a real multiply
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;
    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE exp2 CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR2 ;;

The multiply is real arithmetic, but a native exp would not need it. The constant also takes a vector register and an XMEM row.

The hardware activations (ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE, the architecture spec's list) are identity, relu, relu6, reciprocal, rsqrt, exp2 and generic, which evaluates the table LD.LUT loaded. The emulator-only ACTIVATE.EXACT (FP32 mode only) has the 13 exact functions of activations.py: identity, relu, relu6, sigmoid, tanh, gelu, softplus, elu, exp2, reciprocal, rsqrt, silu and window. Neither has exp, log, sqrt, abs, sign, clamp or pow. reciprocal and rsqrt are native, so no kernel needs a Newton-Raphson divide.

docs.title: A10 — a fractional scalar in a CR
docs.text:
A CR scalar of MULT.VE, MULT.EE or MULT.RC.VE is a MULT constant (see Configuration registers). In the NX8 mode it holds an NX8 element with a scale and an NX type of its own (value[7:0], scale[15:8], fe[19:16], sign[23:20]), so it holds a fractional constant directly: 0.5 is the element 1.0 (value 0) under scale 2^-1 (scale 126). In the FP32 mode it is the float32 bit pattern (0.5 is 0x3F000000). CR0 and CR1 read as 0.0 and 1.0 in both modes.

    MULT.RC.VE LR0 CR3 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # CR3 holds the MULT constant 0.5
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;

docs.title: A11 — ACC.MUL: multiply the accumulator by MULT_RES
docs.text:
ACC.ADD adds MULT_RES to R_ACC. No instruction computes R_ACC[i] *= MULT_RES[i], so the accumulator goes through XMEM (A8) and comes back as a multiplicand.

    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR2 ;; # drain R_ACC
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;;   # reload into R_CYCLIC
    MULT.RC.VV LR0 R0 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;  # multiply by R0
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;

ACC.ADD in place of the round trip computes A + B, not A * B.

docs.title: A12 — post-increment addressing: a load feeds the next word's multiply
docs.text:
MULT.RC.* reads R_CYCLIC at cycle start (timing model), so it cannot use a row loaded in the same instruction word (issue #157). The pointer increment takes an instruction word of its own in each loop iteration, with the MULT slot idle.

loop_pre:
    ADD LR1 LR1 CR1 ;;              # a whole word, no multiply
loop:
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 LR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # real multiply-accumulate
    ACC.ADD ;
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;
    ADD LR2 LR2 CR4 ;
    BLT.S LR1 LR5 loop_pre ;;

A kernel whose loop counter is an AGG dest_slot needs no extra word: dest_slot reads the value after the LR writes of the same word, so the counter starts one lower and its INC shares the word with the AGG (the attn_v_* kernels).

docs.title: A13 — a narrow multiply costs a full one
docs.text:
A kernel that pads a narrow row with zeros to 128 lanes multiplies all 128. No encoding makes a narrow multiply cheaper.

# The same word counts 128 lanes whether 16 or 128 hold data
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 LR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; # CR15.L: valid_elements = 128 (the default)
    ACC.ADD ;;

valid_elements does not gate multiply results: _mult_mask_and_shift gates them with R_MASK and the partition-dependent shift. The lane statistic intersects that mask with the active elements of the multiply's DS half (valid_elements per active partition; CR15.L by convention). AGG instructions use valid_elements to bound their reduction. A narrower declared width changes the lane statistic only, not the results or the cycle count.

docs.title: A14 — one accumulator: MULT.OUTER and many outputs at once
docs.text:
There is one R_ACC, so one output channel is in progress at a time. A kernel reads its whole input block again for each output channel.

j_loop:
    SET LR2 CR2 ;;                  # rewind the data pointer for each output j
    SET LR1 CR5 ;;                  # restart the inner counter
k_loop:
    MULT.RC.VE LR0 LR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;
    ACC.ADD ;
    LD.MULT.CYCLIC LR2 CR0 LR0 ;    # the same rows, read once per output
    ADD LR2 LR2 CR4 ;
    INC LR1 1 ;
    BLT.S LR1 LR5 k_loop ;;
    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR3 ; # output j
    INC LR6 1 ;
    BLT.S LR6 LR7 j_loop ;;

xmem_reads grows by a factor of N_OUT, the number of output channels.

docs.title: A15 — SELECT / MASK.VV, CSEL and a scalar MUL in the LR slot
docs.text:
Three smaller gaps.

# SELECT / MASK.VV: multiply by a 1.0 / 0.0 mask
    LD.MULT R0 LR2 CR2 ;;           # R0 <- keep mask, 1.0 data / 0.0 padding
    MULT.RC.VV LR0 R0 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;  # gate by multiplying
    ACC.ADD ;;

# CSEL: a branch diamond stands in for a conditional move
    BLT.S LR1 LR5 use_full ;;
    SET LR6 CR8 ;;                  # tail bound
    B joined ;;
use_full:
    SET LR6 CR7 ;;                  # full bound
joined:

# Scalar MUL: repeated ADD in place of cbound * P
    ADD LR6 LR6 LR7 ;;
    ADD LR6 LR6 LR7 ;;

The branch diamond costs several instruction words on each path, none of them multiplying.

docs.title: The retired A16: the emulator-only accumulator store
docs.text:
A16 counted ST.ACC, a raw R_ACC dump in an emulator-only slot with no hardware encoding. ADR 0007 removed it: the AaQ stage stores its own row, so a raw dump is ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity (the hardware instruction, quantized in the NX8 mode) or, in the FP32 mode, ACTIVATE.EXACT identity (emulator-only, an exact FP32 row). The number A16 is not reused.

    ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR2 LR2 ;; # NX8: one row and its metadata
    ACTIVATE.EXACT identity CR15.L CR2 LR2 ;;           # FP32 mode only

docs.title: How runs count the idioms
docs.text:
Two mechanisms count idioms, at two levels of detail.

Hit counts, on every run. ipu_emu/isa_alias_spec.py declares the idioms as a table, checked at import. Each run classifies every instruction word against it and reports a count per idiom in RunStats.alias_hits, beside the identity-multiply and lane counters. The table lists the most specific entry first, and the first match wins, so a word that matches several entries counts once, under the most specific.

A constraint can name an instruction in another slot of the same word, since a word executes as a unit. That is the only difference between A1–A4 and A6: each uses the same MULT.RC.VE with a 1.0 scalar or a declared ones vector, and A1–A4 differ in the ACC instruction beside it. A6 wins for a nonzero mask offset, for a mask-zero window narrower than the declared destination span, and for a declared vector routed through ACC.STRIDE. A mask that matches a narrower valid_elements declaration is ordinary padding and does not by itself make a word A6. An unmasked move and a routing with identical operands have the same signature, and count as A1–A4.

A scalar constraint names a supported scalar multiplicand. A match carries at most one immediate constraint and one constraint on another slot; hardware_only stands alone. The table rejects two entries with the same match signature.

The full profile, on request. ipu_emu.alias_profile.AliasProfile runs a detector per idiom (A1–A15) and records instruction sites, examples, participating instruction words and cycles, active lanes and XMEM bytes. It does not change the effective-MAC accounting. The debug how-to shows how to turn it on.

docs.title: Add an idiom
docs.text:
1. To count it on every run, add an entry to the table in ipu_emu/isa_alias_spec.py, most specific entries first.
  2. To profile it, write a detector: a class whose observe(event) yields Match objects. Register its factory and its AliasDefinition in default_registry() in ipu_emu.alias_detectors.
  3. Add tests: a positive and a negative detector test, and the count it gives on a real kernel.

A detector subscribes to slots through its slots tuple; without one it receives every event. A cycle event holds the completed instruction word and its next pc. Event.facts holds the decoded operands and the execution details alias_observer collects. The profiling engine has no per-idiom code, so a new detector needs no change to emulator dispatch or report formatting, unless it needs an execution fact nothing collects yet.

For an experiment, copy default_registry(), register the detector on the copy, and pass it to AliasProfile(registry). Each profile gets its own detector state from the factories. A registry rejects a duplicate ID and a match a detector emits under another detector's ID.

docs.title: Kernel coverage
docs.text: The kernel registry (ipu_harness.registry) answers which kernel computes a given operation with given parameters, and why. It answers from each kernel's own kernel.toml, so no central file holds routing rules: adding a kernel adds its folder or its registry.toml entry and changes nothing else. The tables at the end of this page are generated from the same registry.

docs.title: Why the kernels declare their own domain
docs.text:
A rule written in two places drifts. In the kernels' first form, each kernel's constructor checked its own bounds and a central router restated them, and the two disagreed: softmax_columns_packed advised callers to use softmax_columns for a width of 128 and above long after that boundary had moved to 65. Nothing read the message, so nothing failed.

A kernel's [params] table is the one statement of its domain: each parameter's type, bounds, multiple and choices. The same check (ipu_harness.params.check_params) decides whether a case can run (plan_case) and whether routing accepts a query, so the two cannot disagree.

docs.title: How a kernel declares what it computes
docs.text:
A kernel declares its operation, formats and routing cost in [kernel], and its domain in [params] (kernel.toml reference). From kernels/softmax/softmax_rows_partial/kernel.toml:

[kernel]
op = "softmax"
formats = ["fp32"]
cost = "1 + min(1, max(0, n - 127))"

[params]
rows  = { type = "int", min = 1 }
n     = { type = "int", min = 1, max = 128 }
dim   = { type = "int", choices = [1], default = 1 }

The kernel takes rows of up to 128 elements. At n = 128, where softmax_rows also accepts and is cheaper, its cost rises to 2.

A variant is a kernel that differs from a template kernel only in parameter values. A family declares its variants as entries of kernels/<family>/registry.toml:

[[kernel]]
name = "maxpool2d_nms7"
template = "maxpool2d_nms"
params = { kernel_size = 7, padding = 3 }
doc = "SuperPoint simple_nms, nms_radius = 3"

An entry is its template's kernel.toml with each of the entry's params fixed to one value. The template itself runs its own cases but is not routed: its open domain would tie with each of its entries.

docs.title: How the registry loads
docs.text:
Registry.load reads every kernels/<family>/<name>/kernel.toml and every kernels/<family>/registry.toml. It parses TOML only and imports no kernel Python, so a query never runs kernel code.

A file that fails to load goes into Registry.invalid with its error, and the other kernels still load. The coverage report lists those files: a kernel that failed to load is a kernel missing from coverage, and a registry that stopped at an unrelated half-written kernel would fail when it is most needed. Two kernels with the same name are an error, because a name is one kernel.

docs.title: How a query resolves
docs.text:
Registry.resolve(op, **params) holds no knowledge of any operation. It asks each kernel of the operation whether it accepts the parameters:

  1. Take the kernels whose [kernel] op is op.
  2. Refuse a kernel when the query leaves out a parameter it marks query_required.
  3. Check the parameters against the kernel's domain with check_params, as plan_case does.
  4. With format=, refuse a kernel that does not take the parameters in that format. Without it, refuse a kernel none of whose formats encodes the parameters' element scalars.
  5. Among the kernels that accept, choose the lowest [kernel] cost. A cost is a number or an expression over the integer parameters and derived values.

The verdict names the chosen kernel, its parameters with defaults filled, the formats it runs them in, its Bazel label and the other kernels that accept, cheapest first. When no kernel accepts, the verdict's reason names every kernel's refusal, so the caller learns what was wrong.

Overlapping domains are normal: softmax_rows_partial and softmax_rows both accept n = 128, and cost settles which one runs. Two accepting kernels at the same lowest cost are a ConfigurationError, never settled by name or discovery order, so the answer cannot change because a folder was renamed. A tie between entries that fix a parameter the query leaves out is a refusal that names the parameter, since the query is incomplete rather than the registry wrong.

docs.title: Framework layers
docs.text:
Registry.from_layer(layer, input_shape) takes a framework layer, for example nn.Softmax(dim=1), and the shape it will receive. A layer carries configuration (dim, in_channels, stride) but no shape, and the shape selects the kernel, so both are needed.

A family's adapters are LAYER_ADAPTERS = {"Conv2d": fn, ...} in ipu_kernels.<family>.layers, each mapping (layer, input_shape) to an operation and its parameters. The registry imports a family's adapters by module name the first time from_layer needs one, and matches a layer by its class name, so the registry never imports torch. Adapters follow two rules, because both failures give confident wrong answers:

  • Translate what you understand; refuse the rest. An adapter that ignores an attribute it does not model answers for an operation the kernel does not implement.
  • Never assume a neighbouring layer is equivalent. LogSoftmax and Softmin sit beside Softmax in torch.nn with the same signature; the softmax adapters refuse them by name.

docs.title: Ask the registry from the command line
docs.text:
bazel run //kernels:query                                         # the coverage report
bazel run //kernels:query -- softmax rows=8 n=300 dim=1           # which kernel, and why
bazel run //kernels:query -- softmax rows=8 n=n dim=1 --sweep n=1..139   # where the winner changes

--sweep runs ipu_harness.query.boundaries: it resolves the query at each value and collapses runs of the same winner, which is how a family page's routing table is produced. The table cannot describe behaviour the kernels do not have, because it is probed. The softmax page shows the softmax table. The options are in the command-line reference.

docs.title: What keeps the registry honest
docs.text:
A declarative registry can fail in one new way: a kernel's domain accepts a query the kernel computes wrongly. These tests guard it:

  • Cases. Every kernel's cases run it and compare its output with an independent reference.
  • Routing tests. A family's test_routing.py probes the registry at each boundary its docs page's routing tables claim, including that the winner changes where the table says, and checks that an accepted query also plans and places. A domain that moves without the page fails there.
  • Conformance (softmax, kernels/softmax/test_conformance.py). For each shape, the registry chooses a kernel, and the test runs it against a NumPy reference, so a kernel cannot claim a domain it mishandles.
  • Spec hygiene. Every kernel.toml loads, kernel names are unique, and each family's generated registry.bzl matches its registry.toml.

docs.title: Timing model
docs.text:
The IPU retires one instruction word per cycle, and every slot of the word executes in that cycle. Within a word, a register read sees one of two values:

  • the cycle start value: what the register held when the word began;
  • the forwarded value: what an earlier slot of the same word wrote to it.

The timing contract fixes which of the two each read sees. It has four rules (ADR 0002):

  1. The Control stage (LR, COND) reads LRs at cycle start. Every other stage reads LRs after the LR writes of the same word.
  2. MULT reads R0, R1, R_CYCLIC (and their row metadata) and R_MASK at cycle start.
  3. MULT_RES is forwarded to ACC (including AGG and ACC.RESHAPE). R_ACC is forwarded to AAQ (and to the emulator-only AAQ_EXACT).
  4. The three LR sub-slots read cycle-start values.

A read that no rule names follows the slot order.

ipu_isa.timing declares the contract as data, and every instruction in instruction_spec.py declares the registers it reads and writes. load_isa rejects a declaration that breaks the contract, and the emulator's timing tests check that each handler reads what it declares.

docs.title: Every read, by slot
docs.text:
This table is generated from the declarations in ipu_isa. Selected by names the operands that select the register; implicit is a read that no operand names. R is the R0/R1 pair.
