docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Each example below assembles and runs as a test (docs/examples/test_timing_model.py). The test sets up the state from the # given: comments, runs the program to HALT, and checks every # expect: comment. The examples run in the emulator-only FP32 mode, where an element is its value and a row has no metadata; the timing is the same in the NX8 mode. XMEM[n] is XMEM row n (128 elements); a given sets every element of the row. CR0 is the MULT constant 0 and CR1 is 1 in every run.

docs.title: Rule 1: Control reads LRs at cycle start, other stages after the LR writes
docs.text:
In the first word, INC writes LR0 = 1. BEQ is in the Control stage, so it compares the cycle-start LR0 (0) with CR0 (0) and branches to taken. LD.MULT is in the LOAD stage, so its offset is the new LR0 (1): it loads row CR2 + 1, which holds 2s.

# given: CR2 = 16
# given: XMEM[16] = 1
# given: XMEM[17] = 2
    INC LR0 1 ; LD.MULT R0 LR0 CR2 ; BEQ LR0 CR0 taken ;;
    HALT ;;
taken:
    INC LR7 1 ;;
    HALT ;;
# expect: LR0 == 1
# expect: LR7 == 1
# expect: R0[0] == 2

The same rule gives MULT, ACC, AAQ and AAQ_EXACT their LR operands after the LR writes: an AGG dest_slot or an ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE table_offset sees an LR that the same word increments.

docs.title: Rule 2: MULT reads its data registers at cycle start
docs.text:
The second word loads 5s into R0 and multiplies R0 by CR1 (1). MULT reads R0 at cycle start, so it multiplies the 2s that the first word loaded. The 5s are in R0 after the word, for the next word's MULT. R_CYCLIC, R_MASK and the row metadata LD.MULT copies behave the same way: LD.MULT.CYCLIC or LD.MASK in the same word as a MULT reaches only the next word's MULT.

# given: CR2 = 16
# given: CR3 = 17
# given: XMEM[16] = 2
# given: XMEM[17] = 5
    LD.MULT R0 LR0 CR2 ;;
    LD.MULT R0 LR0 CR3 ; MULT.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ;;
    HALT ;;
# expect: MULT_RES[0] == 2
# expect: R0[0] == 5

docs.title: Rule 3: MULT_RES reaches ACC, and R_ACC reaches AAQ, in the same cycle
docs.text:
The second word multiplies, accumulates, activates and stores in one word. ACC.ADD.FIRST reads this word's MULT_RES (3), and ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE reads this word's R_ACC and writes 3 to XMEM row CR3 (in the NX8 mode it quantizes the row first and writes its metadata too).

# given: CR2 = 16
# given: CR3 = 18
# given: XMEM[16] = 3
    LD.MULT R0 LR0 CR2 ;;
    MULT.VE LR0 CR1 0 LR0 CR15.L CR14.L ; ACC.ADD.FIRST ; ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity CR15.L CR14.L CR3 LR0 ;;
    HALT ;;
# expect: MULT_RES[0] == 3
# expect: R_ACC[0] == 3
# expect: XMEM[18][0] == 3

docs.title: Rule 4: LR sub-slots read cycle-start values
docs.text:
The three LR sub-slots all read before any of them writes. In the second word, ADD reads the cycle-start LR0 (5), not the 6 that INC writes in the same word.

    INC LR0 5 ;;
    INC LR0 1 ; ADD LR1 LR0 CR0 ;;
    HALT ;;
# expect: LR0 == 6
# expect: LR1 == 5

Two LR sub-slots of one word must not write the same LR; the emulator faults on that word (F-3).

docs.title: Slot order
docs.text:
The slots of a word execute in this order: BREAK, LR, LOAD, MULT, ACC, AAQ, AAQ_EXACT, COND. A read that no rule names is forwarded when every slot that writes the register runs earlier in the word, and is at cycle start otherwise:

  • ACTIVATE.EXACT reads R_ACC forwarded: only ACC writes it.
  • ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE reads the AaQ LUT at cycle start: LD.LUT, in its own slot, writes it.
  • ACC.ADD, ACC.SUB, ACC.MAX and the non-FIRST AGG forms read R_ACC at cycle start: their own slot writes it.
  • CR reads are at cycle start: no slot writes a CR during a run.

docs.title: When a kernel needs an extra word
docs.text:
A value that a read sees only at cycle start reaches it one word later. The kernel then spends a word, or arranges the program so the old value is the one it needs:

  • Load, then multiply (rule 2). A MULT cannot use data that the same word's LOAD fetches. Load one word ahead, or software-pipeline the loop so each word multiplies the previous word's load.
  • Branch on a counter (rule 1). A branch compares the counter's value from before the word's INC. The loop below runs four times, not three, and ends with LR0 = 4. Compare against the limit minus one, or increment in an earlier word.
  • Chain LR arithmetic (rule 4). An LR sub-slot cannot use another sub-slot's result from the same word. Put the dependent step in the next word.
# given: CR2 = 3
loop:
    INC LR0 1 ; BNE LR0 CR2 loop ;;
    HALT ;;
# expect: LR0 == 4

The ISA idioms catalogue shows these patterns in the kernels, including the pointer bump that needs an LR-only word (A12).

docs.title: What the emulator does not model
docs.text:
The emulator executes one word per cycle and never stalls. It has no model of the hardware pipeline's stage latencies or of the cache agent's backpressure, so the stall-limit fault F-8 never fires (OQ-28).

The hardware runs each word through six pipelined stages (Architecture and pipeline), and IPU-ARCH-13 requires that pipelining not change any architectural result. The timing contract is that architectural result: it states which values a word sees, whatever the stage latencies. The Control Stage Specification describes the LR forwarding from CTRL to the later stages.

The contract settles two rows of the requirements' open questions (OQ-9 and OQ-10): MULT does not see the same word's load (rule 2), and every stage after CTRL reads LRs after the LR writes (rule 1).

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Go from a fresh clone to a passing test run and one kernel run. Every command runs from the repository root.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linux on x86-64 or ARM64, with git, curl and python3. On Windows, use WSL2; on macOS, see macOS.
  • About 5 GB of free disk for the Bazel cache.

Bazel manages every other tool and Python package. The repository has no C or C++ code, so no compiler is needed.

docs.title: Install the toolchain
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/rechefe/ipu-emulator.git
cd ipu-emulator
./tools/bootstrap.sh

tools/bootstrap.sh installs bazelisk as bazel, at the pinned version and checksum that CI, the dev container and the Claude Code hook also use. Bazelisk then runs the Bazel version in .bazelversion. The script installs into /usr/local/bin, or into ~/.local/bin when /usr/local/bin is not writable; set BIN_DIR to choose. A second run downloads nothing.

Check the install:

bazel version

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
bazel test //...

The first run downloads Bazel, Python and the locked packages (including the ~200 MB PyTorch CPU wheel), then runs the default test tier. On a GitHub-hosted CI runner the test step takes about 20 minutes. Bazel caches results, so a second run with nothing changed takes seconds.

The run passes when bazel test exits 0 and its summary ends N tests pass. Test tiers in the README explains the default and heavy tiers.

docs.title: Run one kernel
docs.text:
Run the QKV projection kernel's default FP32 case:

bazel run //kernels/projections:proj_qkv_144_p4

The run places and packs the kernel's inputs, assembles it, emulates it to HALT and compares the output with the reference. It takes about a minute and prints one line per case and format:

proj_qkv_144_p4/default/fp32: PASS  cycles=572006  MAC util=87.0%  y: max|err|=8.58307e-06 (FP32_LONG)
Field Meaning PASS Every output matched the reference within its tolerance tier. A mismatch prints FAIL, the worst element and its tier instead, and the command exits 1. cycles Instruction words retired. MAC util Multiplier work that was real arithmetic, as a fraction of the run's peak (MAC utilisation). y: Output y: its largest absolute difference from the reference, and the tolerance tier it was held to.

--list-cases lists a kernel's cases, and --case NAME runs one of them. CLI reference lists the other options.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
Page What it covers Write a kernel Write a kernel's program and kernel.toml, then run, test and debug it. Add an instruction Add an instruction to the ISA, the assembler and the emulator. Debug a kernel Step through a kernel in the debugger and inspect registers. Use the reference model from cocotb Drive the emulator as a reference model from an RTL testbench.

The Getting Started guide (PDF) is a printable introduction to the IPU, its assembly language and the emulator. Contributors read Code conventions before writing code.

docs.title: Windows (WSL2)
docs.text:
Install WSL2 with Ubuntu, then follow this page inside it:

wsl --install

Clone into the WSL2 file system (for example ~/ipu-emulator), not under /mnt/c/: Bazel is much slower on the Windows file system.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
tools/bootstrap.sh supports Linux only. Install bazelisk with Homebrew instead; it reads the same .bazelversion:

brew install bazelisk

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
The Dockerfile builds an Ubuntu image with the pinned toolchain from tools/bootstrap.sh:

docker build -t ipu-emulator .
docker run -it --rm -v "$PWD":/workspace ipu-emulator bash

Inside the container, run the commands from Run the tests.

docs.title: VS Code and the dev container
docs.text:
.devcontainer/devcontainer.json builds the same image. Install the Dev Containers extension, open the repository, press F1 and select Dev Containers: Reopen in Container.

VS Code offers the recommended extensions from .vscode/extensions.json, and the dev container installs them:

  • IPU Assembly (yardencarmi.ipu-asm): highlighting, diagnostics, completion and kernel run and debug buttons for .asm files
  • Python and Pylance (Microsoft): Python language support and type checking
  • Ruff (Astral): Python linting and formatting
  • Bazel (BazelBuild): Bazel support
  • GitLess (maattdd): inline Git history
  • Material Icon Theme (PKief): file icons

If IPU Assembly is not in the Marketplace, install the latest build:

curl -LO https://github.com/rechefe/ipu-emulator/releases/download/vscode-latest/ipu-asm.vsix
code --install-extension ipu-asm.vsix

docs.title: Build this documentation
docs.text:
The site builds offline through Bazel:

bazel build --config=docs //docs:build_docs      # writes bazel-bin/docs/site.tar
bazel run --config=docs //docs:serve_docs        # build and serve it locally

--config=docs forwards the optional GISCUS_* overrides into the build. The release log is committed, and a workflow refreshes it on master after every merge. To refresh it by hand:

bazel run //docs:update_release_log -- --recent --output "$PWD/docs/content/release-log.md"

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Fix bazel: command not found after the bootstrap Add the install directory (~/.local/bin when /usr/local/bin was not writable) to PATH. external repository not found Run bazel clean --expunge, then the command again. A kernel run prints error: Run it again with --config=debug to step through it; see Debug a kernel.

docs.title: How-to
docs.text:
These pages are for a user with a task to do. Each one is a set of steps.

Page What it covers Write a kernel Write a kernel's program and kernel.toml, then run, test and debug it. Add an instruction Add an instruction to the ISA, the assembler and the emulator. Debug a kernel Find why a kernel gives a wrong output, faults, or runs slowly. Step through a kernel run Replay a recorded kernel run cycle by cycle in the Cycle Inspector, and add a run to it. Use the reference model from cocotb Drive the emulator as a reference model from an RTL testbench.

docs.title: Add an instruction
docs.text:
An instruction takes three edits: its entry in the ISA package, its handler in the emulator, and a test. Everything else is derived from the entry: the opcode, the instruction word layout, the assembler's parser and encoder, the disassembler, the syntax line, the generated docs, the editor's hover and completion, and the SystemVerilog package.

The "one edit" test proves it. It adds a dummy instruction, TESTNEG, to copies of the sources with only the first two edits, then assembles and runs a program that uses it (src/ipu-emu/test/test_one_edit_end_to_end.py). The examples below are that test's own entry and handler.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Decide three things:

  • The slot the instruction issues in: lr, load, mult, acc, aaq, aaq_exact, cond or break. The Instructions reference lists what each slot holds today.
  • The tag, which the instruction takes from its slot:
    • HARDWARE (every slot but aaq_exact and break) is in the IPU, so it is in the hardware word and the SystemVerilog package.
    • EMULATOR (aaq_exact, break) exists only in the emulator. The assembler rejects it under --target hardware.
    • ASSEMBLER is a pseudo-instruction: the assembler expands it into a real instruction, and it has no opcode. See Pseudo-instructions.
  • The mnemonic, under the standard in the Glossary: control-stage instructions have plain names (ADD, BEQ), datapath ones UNIT.OP[.VARIANT] (LD.MULT, ACC.ADD.FIRST), and none has an underscore.

docs.title: Step 1: the ISA entry
docs.text:
Add the entry to the slot's dictionary in INSTRUCTION_SPEC, in src/ipu-isa/src/ipu_isa/instruction_spec.py. This is TESTNEG at the end of the "lr" dictionary:

        "TESTNEG": {
            "operands": [
                {"name": "dest", "type": "LrIdx", "write": True},
                {"name": "src", "type": "LrIdx", "read": "cycle_start"},
            ],
            "doc": InstructionDoc(
                title="Test negate",
                summary="Negate a local register (a test instruction).",
                operands=[
                    "dest: Destination local register (LR0–LR15)",
                    "src: Source local register (LR0–LR15)",
                ],
                operation="dest = -src",
                example="TESTNEG LR1 LR0;;",
            ),
            "execute_fn": "execute_testneg",
        },
  • operands: the name and type of each operand, in assembly order. A register the instruction reads has "read": "cycle_start" (its value when the word began) or "forwarded" (after earlier slots of the same word wrote it). The register it writes has "write": True. The types are on the Operand types page.
  • implicit_reads, implicit_writes (optional): every register the handler reads or writes that no operand names, such as {"register": "mult_res", "view": "forwarded"}.
  • doc: the title, summary, one line per operand starting with its name, the operation, and an example that assembles. There is no syntax line: it is derived from the mnemonic and the operand names (TESTNEG dest src).
  • execute_fn: the handler's name (step 2).

The opcode is the entry's position in its slot, so append the entry to keep every other opcode where it is; never assign one. The entry is checked when ipu_isa is imported: an unknown key, a misnamed operand line or a read the timing model does not allow raises SpecError with the entry's path, such as lr.TESTNEG.operands[src].read.

docs.title: Step 2: the handler
docs.text:
Add execute_<name> to the module of the instruction's slot, under src/ipu-emu/src/ipu_emu/slots/ (lr.py for lr; aaq_exact.py is aaq_exact; brk.py is break). This is TESTNEG's, in lr.py:

def execute_testneg(ipu: Ipu, *, dest: int, src: int) -> None:
    """Execute TESTNEG: uint32 ``dest = -src``."""
    ipu.state.regfile.set_lr(dest, (-src) & 0xFFFFFFFF)
  • The first parameter is the engine, ipu. The rest are keyword-only (the *), and their names are exactly the operand names of the entry. The emulator binds every entry's execute_fn when it is imported and names any handler that is missing or whose parameters differ.
  • An operand with "read" arrives resolved: an LR or CR as its 32-bit value, a mult-stage register as its bytes, which the handler decodes. One without, such as the register written, an immediate or a label, arrives as its index or value.
  • A vector handler reads its lanes through the active lane codec (ipu.codec, from ipu_emu.numerics), computes on them, and writes the result back through the same codec. It has no branch on the element format. execute_mult_rc_vv in mult.py is a short example.
  • A slot module never imports another one. A helper two slots need goes in ipu_emu/geometry.py or on CycleView; one only this slot uses stays a private function in the module.
  • The handler never raises a fault. If the instruction can fault on register values (an XMEM row out of range, an index the ISA forbids), add check_<name>(ipu, *, <operands>) beside it, with the same parameters, returning (FaultId, detail) or None. The emulator binds it by that name and runs it in each word's check phase, before any slot but LR has run, so a faulting word has no effect (Faults). check_ld_mult_cyclic in load.py is a short example. A fault decided by the encoding alone (a reserved operand code) needs nothing: the emulator finds it at fetch.

docs.title: Step 3: the test
docs.text:
Add a test with the shared emulator test helpers in src/ipu-emu/test/emu_support.py, next to the tests of the same slot in test_execute.py. run assembles a program, runs it to HALT and returns the final state; make_state stops before running, so the test can write XMEM first. A test of ADD, an existing lr instruction:

from emu_support import run

def test_add_sums_two_local_registers():
    """ADD writes src_a + src_b to dest, wrapping at 32 bits."""
    state = run("SET LR0 CR2;; SET LR1 CR3;; ADD LR2 LR0 LR1;; HALT;;", cr={2: 0xFFFFFFFF, 3: 2})
    assert state.regfile.get_lr(2) == 1

docs.title: Step 4: check
docs.text:
bazel test //...

Some tests pin today's ISA, and fail by design once it has one more instruction. Update them; the failing test names what it pins.

  • Baselines regenerate: run tools/update_baselines.sh. For an lr instruction it rewrites nine files besides the conformance suite (whose every trace header names the ISA), among them the generated pages, the editor's data, the decoded field maps and the SystemVerilog golden. Commit them with the reason, as the Baselines rule asks.
  • Facts written by hand are edited:
    • the record of every instruction, src/ipu-isa/test/baselines/spec_snapshot.json;
    • the reserved encodings: the per-slot counts in src/ipu-isa/test/test_faults.py, and the F-1 table in Faults;
    • for an lr instruction, the "one edit" tests' own count of lr instructions (test_one_edit.py in ipu-isa, test_one_edit_generators.py in ipu-gen).
    • for a HARDWARE instruction, its conformance program: an entry in INSTRUCTIONS in src/ipu-emu/test/conformance_cases.py (test_conformance names an instruction no case runs); run tools/update_baselines.sh again to write its cases.
  • An instruction whose opcode does not fit in its slot's opcode field (a slot of 16 instructions getting a 17th) widens the slot, and with it the instruction word. More tests then fail, those that pin widths and the word layout. For a HARDWARE slot it is a breaking change to the wire format (CLAUDE.md, below). The list above is for an instruction that fits.

For a HARDWARE instruction, check the generated SystemVerilog package: a downstream RTL repository vendors it, and its widths are wire format. Follow the Generated SystemVerilog Package section of CLAUDE.md.

For an EMULATOR instruction, check that a program using it is rejected for the hardware:

bazel run //src/ipu-as:ipu-as -- assemble --target hardware --input "$PWD/prog.asm" --output "$PWD/prog.bin"

docs.title: What you do not edit
docs.text:
No code has a list of instructions to extend. The opcode, the assembler's grammar and encoder, the disassembler, the generated pages and the editor's data all follow from the entry. If the code needed an edit beyond the entry and the handler, the "one edit" test would list it in KNOWN_MANUAL_EDITS. That list is empty. Only the tests and pages that pin today's ISA change, as in step 4.

A new operand type is the exception: it needs an entry in src/ipu-isa/src/ipu_isa/operand_types.py, a token class in the assembler's OPERAND_TYPE_MAP (src/ipu-as/src/ipu_as/inst.py). The emulator picks how a read operand resolves from the register banks its domain names (_READ_BY_BANKS in src/ipu-emu/src/ipu_emu/ipu.py); only a type over a new bank needs a read code in ipu_emu/resolver.py. Its field_suffix and sv_typedef are wire format.

docs.title: Pseudo-instructions
docs.text:
When an existing instruction already does the work under another name or operand order, add a pseudo-instruction instead. BGT.S a b label is BLT.S b a label, for example. It needs only an entry in PSEUDO_INSTRUCTION_SPEC, in the same file:

  • operands, as for an instruction;
  • expands_to: the target's slot, its instruction, and its args in order, each one of the pseudo's operand names or a fixed register such as "CR0";
  • doc, as for an instruction.

It has no execute_fn, no opcode and no handler, since the emulator never sees it. The assembler picks a pseudo-instruction by name and operand count, so one may share a name with an instruction of another arity. Its test checks it assembles to the same words as its expansion (in src/ipu-as/test/test_assemble.py):

from ipu_as.lark_tree import assemble

def test_bgt_is_blt_with_its_operands_swapped():
    assert assemble("BGT.S LR0 LR1 +1;;") == assemble("BLT.S LR1 LR0 +1;;")

docs.title: Debug a kernel
docs.text:
Find out why a kernel gives the wrong answer, faults, or runs slowly. Every command runs from the repository root.

The debugger is the kernel runner in a terminal user interface (TUI). Add --config=debug to bazel run on any kernel target. The run assembles the kernel, loads its inputs and CRs, and stops at cycle 0, before the first instruction word runs. It takes the same options as an ordinary run:

bazel run --config=debug //kernels/reshape/identity -- --case single_row
bazel run --config=debug //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --case one_row --format fp32

A kernel target also takes --debug in place of --config=debug. The debugger needs an interactive terminal.

Every key and mouse action is listed in the debugger controls, generated from the debugger's own key table. Press ? in the debugger for the same list.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
The debugger has four panes. Each pane's title starts with the number key that focuses it:

Pane Shows 1 Pipeline Registers R0, R1, R_C, R_MASK, R_ACC, AAQ_ROW (the row the last AaQ store wrote, and in NX8 its metadata), MULT_RES, MEM_BYPASS 2 Instructions The disassembly around the current PC, one instruction per row, with || marking the rest of a word's slots 3 XMEM A range of XMEM rows or bytes; in NX8 each row's marker line shows its metadata (scale, dynamic exponent) 4 CR/LR LR0–LR15 and CR0–CR15

Each pane has tabs. F2 adds a tab and F3 edits the active one; both open an editor at the bottom of the screen. The value it takes depends on the pane:

Pane Tab request Example Instructions current, or a PC from 0 to INST_MEM_SIZE - 1 12 CR/LR all, lr or cr lr XMEM row|byte BASE OFFSET COUNT FORMAT row CR3 0 128 f32 Pipeline Registers A register name R_ACC

In an XMEM request, BASE and OFFSET are each an immediate, an LR or a CR; the debugger adds their values when it draws the pane, so a tab follows the registers as they change. row addresses XMEM rows, byte addresses bytes. COUNT is in values of FORMAT: bytes for hex, int8 and u8, 16-bit values for cell16, 32-bit values for u32 and f32.

A value that changed since the last stop is bold and underlined.

docs.title: The output is wrong
docs.text:
A wrong output prints FAIL and the worst element:

scale/one_row/fp32: FAIL  cycles=7  MAC util=14.3%  y: FAIL at EXACT (max|err|=3 max rel=1); worst at [0, 10]: got 0.0, want 3.0

want is the reference rounded to the case's variant (in NX8, quantized row by row). worst at [0, 10] is the output element (row 0, lane 10) with the largest error.

  1. Run the failing case, in the failing variant, in the debugger:

    bazel run --config=debug //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --case one_row --format fp32

  2. Stop where the output is computed. Choose one:

    • Focus Instructions (2), move the cursor to the word, and press F9 to set a breakpoint on it. A red B marks it. Press F5 to run to it.
    • Move the cursor to the word and press F10 to run to it once.

    • Add a BREAK instruction to the source, then rerun. BREAK stops every time its word issues; BREAK.IFEQ stops only when an LR holds a value, which stops a loop on one iteration:

      row_loop:
    BREAK.IFEQ LR1 3 ;
    LD.MULT R0 LR1 CR2 ;;
    BLT.S LR1 CR4 row_loop ;;
    HALT ;;

      BREAK is emulator-only: remove it before you assemble with --target hardware.

  3. Press F8 to run one instruction word at a time. The debugger stops before each word runs, so the panes show the state that word reads.

  4. Check the scalars in CR/LR (4). Each region base and parameter is in the CR the kernel's ABI names ([abi] in kernel.toml). An LR that drives an address or a loop count must hold the value you expect.

  5. Check the vectors in Pipeline Registers (1) and the data in XMEM (3). Press F2 in XMEM and request the region, for example row CR3 0 128 f32 for an output region whose base row is in CR3. Press f to cycle the tab's format until it matches the run's mode:

    Mode XMEM and R0, R1 MULT_RES, R_ACC FP32 f32 f32 NX8 hex or int8 (the 8-bit codes) f32

    The debugger shows NX8 codes as bytes. Each code's value also needs its row's metadata word, which the XMEM pane shows on each row's marker line and the AAQ_ROW tab in its title. Element formats explains how to decode them, and the accumulator registers are already FP32.

  6. Compare the values with the reference. To get the whole output as a file, run the case without the debugger and add --output. It writes the output even when the comparison fails: --output DIR writes DIR/<name>.npy for each output.

  7. To test a fix without editing the source, press e on a value to change it, then continue. In Instructions, e sets the PC. CR0 and CR1 are read-only.

q or Ctrl-C quits. A quit run prints QUIT (no result) and checks no output. A run that reaches HALT closes the debugger and checks its outputs as an ordinary run does.

docs.title: A fault halted the run
docs.text:
A fault stops the run at the faulting word and prints its code and PC:

scale/one_row/fp32: FAIL  cycles=6  MAC util=16.7%  fault F-2 at PC 6

The debugger also closes on a fault and prints this line.

  1. Look up the code in the fault list. In the emulator says what the emulator checks for each code.

  2. Faults are precise: the faulting word changes no register and no XMEM byte. Run the case in the debugger and stop before the faulting word: press F2 in Instructions, request its PC, and press F9 on it, then F5.

  3. Read the operands the fault checks. For example, F-4 checks the LD.MULT.CYCLIC index, and F-6 checks the XMEM row a load or store addresses (base plus offset, from CR/LR).

  4. Some faults are reached rather than raised by the word at the PC:

    Fault Where to look F-2 The PC is past the program. The word before it fell through, or a branch jumped there; check for a missing HALT or a wrong branch target. F-9 The run reached its cycle limit. A loop counter that never reaches its bound is the usual cause. --max-cycles N sets the limit for one run; 0 disables it.

docs.title: The kernel is too slow
docs.text:
1. Read the run's statistics. A kernel prints its cycle count and MAC utilisation on the result line (the run statistics say what they count):

    scale/default/fp32: PASS  cycles=22  MAC util=18.2%  y: max|err|=0 (EXACT)

    cycles is the number of instruction words retired. MAC util is the multiplier work that was real arithmetic, as a fraction of the run's peak. Multiplies by a constant 1, which only move data, do not count.

  2. Find the instruction sequences that stand in for missing instructions. Add --profile-aliases to the run:

    bazel run //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --case default --format fp32 --profile-aliases

    It prints one line per ISA idiom: how often it occurred and how many cycles took part.

    --- Full ISA measurements (overlapping; no savings estimates) ---
A1_MOV_RC: no observed match
A12_ADDRESSING/load_to_mult: 4 occurrences (verified), 8 participating cycles
A13_NARROW_MULT/lanes_128: 4 occurrences (verified), 4 participating cycles

    The counts overlap: one word can take part in several idioms, so do not add them up.

  3. For the full measurements (instruction sites, examples, lanes, XMEM bytes), write them as JSON with --alias-report FILE in place of --profile-aliases. For a kernel under kernels/ run with --format all, each format writes FILE.<format>.json.

    The report lists every idiom, with counts per subtype and status, instruction sites, a bounded set of examples, participating instruction words and cycles, elapsed spans, active lanes and XMEM bytes. Each occurrence's figures are inclusive: a constant loaded once can take part in many occurrences, so do not sum their costs. overlap_instruction_groups and the unique instruction and cycle totals show the shared words. unique_read_bytes is the union of the addresses read.

  4. To profile a run from Python, attach a profile to the reference model before running it, then read profile.to_dict() or profile.to_json():

    from ipu_emu.alias_profile import AliasProfile

profile = AliasProfile(metadata={"experiment": "hardware-baseline"})
model.attach_alias_profile(profile)  # model: an ipu_emu.reference.ReferenceModel

docs.title: Look at a recorded run in the browser
docs.text: The Cycle Inspector replays a recorded run cycle by cycle, forward and back, with no terminal. It holds traces of a curated set of kernels, and explains how to record a trace of your own case.

docs.title: Use the reference model from cocotb
docs.text:
This page shows how to drive the emulator as a reference model from a cocotb testbench, and compare the RTL with it in three ways: word by word (lockstep), at the end of a run, or through a trace file read offline.

The reference model is ipu_emu.reference.ReferenceModel. Its names and the commit records its step() returns are the stable part of the emulator: they change only with a version bump of API_VERSION, and a breaking change bumps the major number. The rest of ipu_emu can change in any release. The Reference model API page lists every method and rule; each call below links to its entry there.

Every Python block on this page comes from docs/examples/test_reference_model_cocotb.py. bazel test //docs:test_reference_model_cocotb runs that file with a second model as the DUT, so the code shown here runs as written.

docs.title: Step 1: put the model on the testbench's path
docs.text:
The model is pure Python. It needs ipu_emu, ipu_isa and numpy. It does not need the assembler, a simulator or a build step.

  • Bazel testbench. Depend on //src/ipu-emu:ipu_emu_lib. It brings in //src/ipu-isa:ipu_isa_lib.
  • Any other cocotb flow (a Makefile, a CI script). No wheel is published. Check out this repository at a fixed commit and add its two source directories to PYTHONPATH, in the environment that runs the simulator:
export PYTHONPATH="$IPU_EMULATOR/src/ipu-emu/src:$IPU_EMULATOR/src/ipu-isa/src:$PYTHONPATH"
pip install numpy

$IPU_EMULATOR is the checkout. Without the Bazel build flag, prototyping mode is off, which is what a reference model needs.

Assemble the program the RTL runs into a program file:

bazel run //src/ipu-as:ipu-as -- assemble --input "$PWD/prog.asm" --output "$PWD/prog.bin"

docs.title: Step 2: give the model and the RTL the same starting state
docs.text:
reset(fmt) sets the element format (ElementFormat: NX8, the hardware mode, or the emulator-only FP32) and the reset values (CR15.L holds the default DS). load_program takes the program file's bytes. Then write the registers (write_register) and XMEM (write_xmem) the test needs. Writes are allowed only while the model is halted, which it is after a reset or a program load.

import hashlib
import json
import struct
from collections.abc import Awaitable, Callable
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from ipu_emu.reference import ReferenceModel, RunState
from ipu_emu.trace import EMULATOR_VERSION, TraceWriter
from ipu_isa.cr_halves import pack_halves, qf
from ipu_isa.formats import ElementFormat
from ipu_isa.nx8 import Nx8Format
from ipu_isa.trace_schema import SCHEMA_VERSION, isa_digest

FMT = ElementFormat.NX8  # the hardware mode
ROW = 128  # XMEM bytes per row
E4 = Nx8Format(sign=1, exp_format=4, num_bits=8)


def prepare(target: ReferenceModel, program: bytes) -> None:
    """Reset *target*, load *program* and write the starting state."""
    target.reset(FMT)
    target.load_program(program)  # a program file's bytes
    target.write_register("cr", 12, index=2)  # CR2: stop after row 8
    target.write_register("cr", 0, index=3)  # CR3: base row 0
    target.write_register("cr", pack_halves(qf(E4)), index=14)  # CR14.L: the QF
    target.write_register("r_acc", struct.pack("<128f", *[1.0] * 128))
    target.write_xmem(0, b"\xff" * (16 * ROW))  # rows 0-15

Write the same values into the RTL, over AXI or by backdoor. CR0 and CR1 are constants and cannot be written. A register is named by its bank, as ipu_isa.registers names them (lr, cr, r, r_meta, r_cyclic_meta, r_acc, aaq_lut, ...), and an index within the bank. lr and cr take and return unsigned 32-bit ints; the other banks take and return bytes.

docs.title: Step 3: compare word by word (lockstep)
docs.text:
A lockstep comparison calls step() once for each word the RTL retires, and compares the model's commit record (CommitRecord.to_json()) with the one the RTL's retire monitor builds.

Your testbench provides the monitor: a coroutine (rtl_retire below) that awaits the next retired word and returns it as a dict with the commit record's fields. Their JSON form is defined by src/ipu-isa/src/ipu_isa/schemas/commit_record.v1.json (every field):

Field What it holds cycle The words retired since the last reset() or load_program(), before this one. pc_before, pc_after The word's PC, and the PC of the next word. slots Each non-NOP op: {"slot", "mnemonic", "fields"}, fields being the encoded operand values by operand name. reg_writes Each register the word wrote, at its end-of-cycle value: {"register", "index", "value"} for lr and cr, {"register", "offset", "data"} (hex bytes) for a vector register. xmem_writes Each XMEM write: {"address", "data"}, the data as hex bytes. outcome retired, halt (a HALT word) or fault. fault {"id", "pc"} when the word faulted ("F-3", ...), else null. arith_events The arithmetic events the word raised.

A write that leaves a value unchanged is still a write. A faulting word has no slots and no writes: nothing of it retires.

The comparison loop stops at the first halt or fault record. It names the word, its PC and the first field that differs:

#: The commit record's fields. Leave out the ones your monitor cannot see.
FIELDS = (
    "cycle",
    "pc_before",
    "pc_after",
    "slots",
    "reg_writes",
    "xmem_writes",
    "outcome",
    "fault",
    "arith_events",
    "xmem_meta_writes",
)


async def lockstep(
    model: ReferenceModel,
    retire: Callable[[], Awaitable[dict[str, Any]]],
    fields: tuple[str, ...] = FIELDS,
    max_words: int = 100_000,
) -> int:
    """Step *model* once per word the RTL retires and compare the two records.

    Args:
        model: The reference model, prepared like the RTL.
        retire: Awaits the RTL's next retired word, as a commit record dict.
        fields: The record fields to compare.
        max_words: Fail if no HALT or fault comes within this many words.

    Returns:
        The number of words compared.
    """
    for _ in range(max_words):
        expected = model.step().to_json()
        actual = await retire()
        for field in fields:
            if actual.get(field) != expected.get(field):  # a record may omit an empty list
                raise AssertionError(
                    f"word {expected['cycle']} (PC {expected['pc_before']}) {field}: "
                    f"model {expected.get(field)!r}, RTL {actual.get(field)!r}"
                )
        if expected["outcome"] != "retired":  # "halt" or "fault": the run is over
            return expected["cycle"] + 1
    raise AssertionError(f"no HALT within {max_words} words")

If your monitor cannot see a field, such as slots, pass fields without it.

The cocotb test prepares both sides and runs the loop, then checks status for RunState HALTED. load_rtl and rtl_retire are your testbench's coroutines:

import cocotb

@cocotb.test()
async def kernel_lockstep(dut):
    program = Path("prog.bin").read_bytes()  # ipu-as assemble --output prog.bin
    model = ReferenceModel()
    prepare(model, program)
    await load_rtl(dut, program)  # your testbench: the same program and state
    words = await lockstep(model, lambda: rtl_retire(dut))
    assert model.status.state is RunState.HALTED, f"after {words} words: {model.status}"

A BREAK slot never stops step(): the word retires, so the outcome break does not occur. If the RTL stops at a breakpoint, resume it in the monitor before it reports the word.

docs.title: Step 4: compare at the end of a run
docs.text:
When the RTL cannot report each word, run both to the end and compare the state. run() steps until a HALT word, a fault, or the cycle limit, and returns a RunResult: the final status and the number of words retired (cycles). Then read the registers (read_register) and XMEM (read_xmem) to compare. Compare that count with the words the RTL retired, not with its clock cycles: the RTL can stall, the model does not.

async def compare_final_state(model, dut, xmem_rows: range) -> None:
    """Run both to the end, then compare the LRs, the CRs and XMEM rows."""
    result = model.run()
    words = await rtl_run(dut)  # your testbench: start the RTL, await done
    assert words == result.cycles, f"RTL retired {words} words, model {result.cycles}"
    for bank in ("lr", "cr"):
        for index in range(16):
            want = model.read_register(bank, index)
            got = await rtl_read_register(dut, bank, index)
            assert got == want, f"{bank.upper()}{index}: model {want:#x}, RTL {got:#x}"
    for row in xmem_rows:
        want = model.read_xmem(row * ROW, ROW)
        got = await rtl_read_xmem(dut, row * ROW, ROW)
        assert got == want, f"XMEM row {row}: model {want.hex()}, RTL {got.hex()}"


@cocotb.test()
async def kernel_end_of_run(dut):
    program = Path("prog.bin").read_bytes()
    model = ReferenceModel()
    prepare(model, program)
    await load_rtl(dut, program)
    await compare_final_state(model, dut, range(16))

rtl_run, rtl_read_register and rtl_read_xmem are your testbench's coroutines: start the RTL and await its done signal, and read a register or XMEM range by backdoor.

docs.title: Step 5: compare traces offline
docs.text:
A trace is a JSON Lines file: a header line (ipu_isa/schemas/trace.v1.json), then one commit record per word. Pass a TraceWriter to run() to write the model's trace as each word retires. The header's fields come from SCHEMA_VERSION, isa_digest() and EMULATOR_VERSION:

def write_model_trace(program: bytes, path: Path) -> None:
    """Run the model and write its trace: a header line, then one record per word."""
    model = ReferenceModel()
    prepare(model, program)
    header = {
        "schema_version": SCHEMA_VERSION,
        "isa_digest": isa_digest(),
        "format": FMT.value,
        "program_digest": hashlib.sha256(program).hexdigest(),
        "emulator_version": EMULATOR_VERSION,
    }
    with TraceWriter(path, header) as trace:
        model.run(trace=trace)

In a trace, a record's cycle counts the records before it. The program digest is the SHA-256 of the program file.

Have the RTL testbench write the same format, then compare the two files after the simulation. The comparison reads plain JSON, so it needs nothing from the emulator:

#: Header fields that say what the run was; `emulator_version` names the producer.
HEADER_FIELDS = ("schema_version", "isa_digest", "format", "program_digest")


def first_trace_difference(model_trace: Path, rtl_trace: Path) -> str | None:
    """The first difference between two traces, or None when they agree."""
    model_header, *model_records = map(json.loads, model_trace.read_text().splitlines())
    rtl_header, *rtl_records = map(json.loads, rtl_trace.read_text().splitlines())
    for field in HEADER_FIELDS:
        if rtl_header.get(field) != model_header[field]:
            return f"header {field}: model {model_header[field]!r}, RTL {rtl_header.get(field)!r}"
    for want, got in zip(model_records, rtl_records, strict=False):
        if got != want:
            return f"record {want['cycle']}: model {want}, RTL {got}"
    if len(rtl_records) != len(model_records):
        return f"model {len(model_records)} records, RTL {len(rtl_records)}"
    return None

The conformance suite in src/ipu-isa/conformance/ holds a program, starting state and expected trace for every hardware instruction, timing probe and modelled fault. Its README.md says how a testbench runs each case; skip the cases marked emulator_only.

docs.title: What the model does not model
docs.text:
Compare only what the model defines. It does not model:

  • Timing. The model retires one word per cycle and never stalls. It has no pipeline latencies and no cache-agent backpressure, so compare words retired, not clock cycles (Timing model).
  • F-8, the word stall limit. With no stall model it never fires (OQ-28 in Open questions). Clearing its enable bit changes nothing.
  • F-7. There is no table configuration, so no table is read-only or write-only (Faults).
  • The AaQ LUT. ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE quantizes and stores as the AaQ architecture spec says, but evaluates every activation with exact math: LD.LUT stores the LUT bits exactly, and the 17-bit entry format is not published yet, so a generic activation (and any activation an RTL evaluates through its LUT) can differ from the model in the last bits (OQ-38 in Open questions).
  • The disabled behaviour of F-2 to F-6. set_fault_enable refuses to clear their enable bits (OQ-2 in Open questions).

The model also has behaviour the hardware does not. Skip it in an RTL test: the FP32 mode, the r_wide_debug and r_cyclic_wide_debug banks, and the emulator-only aaq_exact slot (ACTIVATE.EXACT). In a commit record, a slot op or register write of these carries "tag": "emulator".

docs.title: Cycle Inspector
docs.text:
The Cycle Inspector replays a recorded kernel run cycle by cycle, in the browser, with nothing to install. Pick a kernel, then step forward and back, run to a breakpoint, or drag the timeline. For each cycle it shows:

  • the program listing, with the instruction word that just ran highlighted and how often each word ran;
  • the instruction word: each slot's instruction and the word's bit fields, MSB first;
  • the register file after the cycle (LR, CR and the vector registers), with the cells the cycle changed outlined; in the NX8 hardware mode each element is shown at its value, decoded with its row's metadata word (scale and dynamic exponent), which the panel lists;
  • the hardware pipeline: which blocks the word used, or each word's stage timing;
  • the XMEM traffic, with the metadata word each AaQ store writes, and the multiplier lanes in use.

The Assembly source tab shows the kernel's .asm file as written, before Jinja rendering. The ISA reference tab lists every instruction of each slot; select one for its full description.

The page is static HTML and JavaScript. It makes no request outside the docs site and uses system fonts.

docs.title: Where the traces come from
docs.text:
Every trace is a build output; none is checked in. The docs build records each curated case with the reference model's trace writer and converts it to the page's format, so the page always matches the current ISA and kernels:

  1. The kernel runner (//src/ipu-harness:run_kernel with --trace and --context) runs a kernel-tree case exactly as its test runs it. It writes the case's trace (one commit record per retired word; the schemas are in ipu_isa/schemas/) and a context file: the variant the case ran in, the kernel's source and labels, the starting registers, and per word the multiplier lanes used and the XMEM ranges read.
  2. ipu-gen inspector-trace converts the two files into the page's JSON (ipu_gen/schemas/inspector-trace.schema.json). It keeps the first 5000 cycles of a long run and marks the trace as truncated.
  3. //docs/inspector:inspector_data gathers every trace, the kernel list (kernels.json, from docs/inspector/curated.toml) and isa.json, the instruction reference the editor extension also reads. The docs build copies them to inspector/data/.

The kernel_trace macro in docs/inspector/defs.bzl does steps 1 and 2 for one case. To record a trace by hand:

bazel run //src/ipu-harness:run_kernel -- kernels/conformance/vector_tour --case e4 --trace "$PWD/trace.jsonl" --context "$PWD/context.json"
bazel run //src/ipu-gen:ipu-gen -- inspector-trace "$PWD/trace.jsonl" "$PWD/context.json" "$PWD/tour_e4.json"

docs.title: Add a kernel
docs.text:
1. Add an entry to CURATED in docs/inspector/BUILD.bazel, where the page's order is kept. Each entry becomes one kernel_trace target, and its name is the kernel's id on the page:

    {"name": "tour_e4", "kernel": "//kernels/conformance/vector_tour", "case": "e4"},

    kernel is a kernel-tree label (//kernels/conformance/vector_tour, or //kernels/<family>:<entry> for a registry entry). case picks one of the kernel's cases (default unless given); to record other values, add a case to the kernel. The case runs in its first format unless format names another, as fc_e4 does: {"name": "fc_e4", "kernel": "//kernels/linear/fully_connected", "format": "e4"}.

  2. Add a [[kernel]] entry with the same id, at the same place, to docs/inspector/curated.toml, with its group (hardware for an NX8 variant, emulator for the emulator-only FP32 mode; ADR 0007), title, label and description.

bazel test //docs/inspector:test_kernels fails when the two lists disagree. bazel build --config=docs //docs:build_docs then rebuilds the site, and bazel test //docs:test_inspector_site checks that the page and every trace are in it.

docs.title: Write a kernel
docs.text:
Write a kernel, the program and its declaration, then run, test and debug it. The example is scale, which multiplies a matrix by a scalar: y = x * s. It is the kernel in kernels/elementwise/scale/, so every listing below is a file you can open. Every command runs from the repository root.

A kernel is a folder with three files the kernel harness reads, plus its Bazel file:

File What it holds scale.asm The program: an assembly template, rendered for each case. kernel.toml Everything else: parameters, regions, registers, cases, tolerances. reference.py What the outputs should be, in PyTorch. BUILD.bazel One line, ipu_kernel(), which declares the targets.

The harness does the rest. From kernel.toml it checks the parameters, places each region in XMEM, writes the inputs in the variant of the run (in NX8, each row with its metadata word), programs the CRs, runs the program and compares the outputs with the reference. A kernel has no Python harness and no hand-written CR setup. Every input is a tensor declared in kernel.toml: a kernel never supplies its XMEM contents ready-made. To see the raw rows a run lays out, open the run in the debugger and read the XMEM pane (Debug a kernel, step 5).

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Pick the family: a folder under kernels/, such as elementwise. A new family is a folder with a BUILD.bazel of load("//kernels:defs.bzl", "ipu_kernel_family") and ipu_kernel_family().
  • Read the assembly syntax if you have not written IPU assembly before, and keep the instruction reference open: step 2 uses nine instructions. Both pages are generated in the docs build.

docs.title: 1. Create the folder
docs.text:
Create kernels/elementwise/scale/ and its BUILD.bazel:

load("//kernels:defs.bzl", "ipu_kernel")

ipu_kernel()

Then add the kernel to its family in kernels/families.bzl:

KERNELS = {
    "elementwise": ["scale"],
}

Bazel cannot find subpackages on its own, so //kernels:test_families fails until the folder is listed.

docs.title: 2. Write the program
docs.text:
scale.asm loads one row of x (128 elements), multiplies it by s, and stores the product, once per row:

{#- scale.asm -- y = x * s, one XMEM row (128 elements) per iteration.

    Design notes
    - MULT.VE multiplies the row in R0 by the MULT constant in {{ cr.s }}
      (float32 bits in FP32; ADR 0007), reading R0 with the QF half in
      {{ cr.qf }}.L (FP32 ignores it).
    - The product goes through ACC (first add), and ACTIVATE.EXACT identity
      stores the accumulator vector: one FP32 row per iteration.
    - Region bases and the row count are in rows, not bytes.
-#}
    SET LR0 CR0 ;
    SET LR1 CR0 ;
    SET LR2 CR0 ;;
row_loop:
    LD.MULT R0 LR1 {{ cr.x }} ;;
    MULT.VE LR0 {{ cr.s }} 0 LR0 CR15.L {{ cr.qf }}.L ;
    ACC.ADD.FIRST ;;
    ACTIVATE.EXACT identity CR15.L {{ cr.y }} LR2 ;;
    ADD LR1 LR1 CR1 ;
    INC LR2 1 ;;
    BLT.S LR1 {{ cr.rows }} row_loop ;;
    HALT ;;

An instruction word is one line ending in ;;; instructions joined by ; issue together in that word. Line by line:

Word What it does SET LR0 CR0 ; SET LR1 CR0 ; SET LR2 CR0 Zero three loop registers: LR0 (an offset that stays 0), LR1 (the row of x) and LR2 (the row of y). CR0 always reads 0. LD.MULT R0 LR1 {{ cr.x }} Load XMEM row x + LR1 into R0. A row is 128 elements in both modes. MULT.VE LR0 {{ cr.s }} 0 LR0 CR15.L {{ cr.qf }}.L ; ACC.ADD.FIRST Multiply R0, from element LR0 (0), by the MULT constant in {{ cr.s }}, with mask slot 0 and no mask shift (every lane, as R_MASK resets), the DS half CR15.L and the QF half {{ cr.qf }}.L (which FP32 ignores). ACC.ADD.FIRST in the same word writes that product to the accumulator. ACTIVATE.EXACT identity CR15.L {{ cr.y }} LR2 Store the accumulator, unchanged, as one FP32 row at y + LR2. ADD LR1 LR1 CR1 ; INC LR2 1 Step to the next row of x (CR1 always reads 1) and of y. BLT.S LR1 {{ cr.rows }} row_loop Loop while LR1 is less than rows. HALT End the run.

LD.MULT has its own word because the multiply does not see a load from the same word; ACC.ADD.FIRST does see the same word's product, and ACTIVATE.EXACT the same word's accumulator. The timing model gives every such rule.

Three things make it a kernel program rather than a fixed one:

  • The header is a {#- ... -#} comment: the first line says what the program computes, then its design notes. The kernel's generated page shows it, so write the notes there, not in a separate file.
  • {{ cr.x }} is the register kernel.toml binds to x. The program never names a CR for a value; it asks for the value by name, and renders as CR2 here. A name the [abi] table does not bind is an error at the line that uses it.
  • Template values: every parameter ({{ rows }}), the variant of the run (format, such as "e4" or "fp32") and each tensor's shape (shapes.x). Every load and store moves one row in both modes, so scale needs none of them.

CR0 reads 0, CR1 reads 1 and CR15.L holds the DS half (by default all 128 elements are valid). scale stores with ACTIVATE.EXACT, the emulator-only exact store, so it runs in the FP32 mode only; an NX8 kernel stores with ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE, which quantizes each row to the case's QF (ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE, ACTIVATE.EXACT and LD.LUT). Mnemonics and register names are upper case, and operands are separated by spaces.

docs.title: 3. Declare it in kernel.toml
docs.text:
The listing is the kernel's own file, included in the docs build, so it is always the one the tests run:

[kernel]
op = "scale"
formats = ["fp32"]                        # FP32 only (ADR 0007); test/scales/scale_rows runs NX8

[params]
rows = { type = "int", min = 1, max = 256 }
s    = { type = "float" }                 # MULT constant: its float32 bits in FP32

[inputs.x]
shape = ["rows", 128]                     # automatic placement; add row = N to pin

[outputs.y]
shape = ["rows", 128]                     # ACTIVATE.EXACT identity: one FP32 row per iteration

[derived]
qf = "case_qf"                            # the case's QF half (0 in FP32, which ignores it)

[abi]                                     # name -> CR; templates see {{ cr.x }} == "CR2"
x    = "CR2"
y    = "CR3"
rows = "CR4"
s    = "CR5"
qf   = "CR6"

[golden]
reference = "reference.py:reference"
tolerance = { fp32 = "EXACT" }

[cases.default]
rows = 4
s = 2.0

[cases.one_row]
rows = 1
s = -3.0

[cases.sweep]                             # one case per value: sweep[rows=1], sweep[rows=7], ...
rows = [1, 7, 33, 128]
s = 1.5

[cases.mine]                              # user data instead of the generator / reference
rows = 2
s = 2.0
inputs = { x = "data/x.npy" }             # small integers in [-8, 8]
expected = { y = "data/y.npy" }           # so y = 2x is exact

Section by section:

  • [kernel]: op is the operation the kernel computes, the name routing answers a query with. formats lists the variants it runs in: fp32 for the emulator-only FP32 mode, an NX8 type (e1 to e7, dynamic, s<sign>e<fe>w<bits>) for the hardware mode. Each case runs in every one of them unless it narrows the list.
  • [params]: each parameter's type and domain. A case or a query outside the domain is refused before anything runs, with the reason. A float parameter bound to a CR is a MULT constant: its float32 bits in FP32, and in NX8 one element with its own scale and type; a value NX8 cannot hold exactly is an error that names the nearest values.
  • [inputs.x] and [outputs.y]: each region's shape, in elements, with expressions over parameters ("rows", "ceil(k / 128)"). The framework places them in XMEM; row = N pins one. Every store writes one row of the mode, so an output is read back in the variant of the run.
  • [derived]: values computed from the case; case_qf is the QF half of the case's variant (0 in FP32), and ds(...), qf(...) and constant(...) build the other CR halves and constants.
  • [abi]: which register holds each value: a region's base row, an integer, or an element scalar. Every region must be bound, since the program can reach it only through a register: by itself, or through a bound [derived] value that reads its base().
  • [golden]: the reference function and the tolerance tier per variant (step 7).
  • [cases.*]: named sets of parameter values. [cases.default] is required. A list makes a sweep: sweep runs as sweep[rows=1], sweep[rows=7] and so on. mine replaces the generated input and the reference with files from data/.

Every key is listed in the kernel.toml reference.

docs.title: 4. Write the reference
docs.text:
reference.py takes the inputs as tensors, already decoded from the variant of the run, and every parameter as a keyword. It returns each output by name:

import torch


def reference(x: torch.Tensor, *, rows: int, s: float) -> dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
    """y = x * s. The framework passes inputs decoded from the case's variant
    and rounds the result to it before comparing."""
    return {"y": x * s}

The harness rounds the result to the variant of the run before it compares: in NX8 it quantizes each golden row as ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE does. An operation other kernels share has one reference in ipu_kernels.reference.ops instead; the kernel names it with [golden] op = "<name>" and needs no reference.py. The second worked example, kernels/reshape/identity/ (y = x), does that: its kernel.toml has op = "identity", and its cases keep their data in a gen.py generator.

docs.title: Test against your own data
docs.text: A case can name its own files instead: inputs replaces the generated input, and expected replaces the reference for that output. scale's mine case reads both from data/, saved with numpy.save in the tensor's shape ([rows, 128]). Each file is rounded to the variant of the run, so pick values it holds exactly, as mine does (small integers), or the comparison sees the rounding. To try other data without editing kernel.toml, pass --input x=my_x.npy to a run (step 6).

docs.title: 5. Run its tests
docs.text:
bazel test //kernels/elementwise/scale

The target runs every case in every variant it runs in, as one test each: test_case[default-fp32], test_case[one_row-fp32], test_case[sweep[rows=7]-fp32]. A failing test reports the case, the variant, the output, the worst element and the tier it failed at, in the same line a run prints. For example, mine run with one element of x changed (--input, step 6):

scale/mine/fp32: FAIL  cycles=12  MAC util=16.7%  y: FAIL at EXACT (max|err|=2 max rel=0.166667); worst at [1, 5]: got 14.0, want 12.0

Row 1, lane 5 of y is 14 where 2 * x is 12. A run that faults instead names the fault, the PC and the source line of the word.

A case with tier = "nightly" runs in //kernels/elementwise/scale:scale_nightly instead, which only the nightly run (--config=full) runs.

docs.title: 6. Run one case
docs.text:
bazel run on the same target runs one case through the kernel runner and prints one report per variant: the result, the cycle count and each output's comparison.

bazel run //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --case one_row --format fp32
bazel run //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --list-cases
bazel run //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --case default --format all

Options to look inside a run:

To Add Use your own input --input x=x.npy Keep the outputs --output out (one .npy per output) Record every cycle --trace trace.jsonl Step through it in the debugger --debug Count the ISA idioms it uses --profile-aliases

For example:

bazel run //kernels/elementwise/scale -- --case one_row --format fp32 --debug

Relative paths are read from where you run the command. Every option is in the command-line reference.

When an output is wrong, run the failing case with --debug: the debugger stops before the first word, and you step through the program watching the registers, the accumulator and XMEM, with the source line of each word. Debug a kernel walks through it, and the Cycle Inspector shows a recorded run in the browser.

docs.title: 7. Choose a tolerance tier
docs.text:
[golden] tolerance names the tier each variant is compared at; a variant not listed is compared at EXACT. The key is a variant name (fp32, e4) or the mode nx8 for every NX8 variant. A key the kernel does not run in is an error that says so. The tiers:

Tier For EXACT Data movement, or one correctly rounded operation. FP32_ORDER FP32 sums whose order differs from the reference's. FP32_LONG Long reductions (K of 256 or more), reciprocal and square-root chains. TRANSCENDENT Exponentials, logarithms and other functions the hardware approximates. NX8_STEP One step of the NX8 golden row's grid: the scale and the element type set the step.

Start from the strictest tier that passes, and say why. A tier's numbers can be overridden for one variant, with the reason. For a kernel whose e4 rows round twice: e4 = { tier = "NX8_STEP", ulps = 2, why = "two roundings: the product and the store" }.

docs.title: Add an NX8 variant to an FP32 kernel
docs.text:
A kernel written for the FP32 mode runs on the hardware only once it runs in NX8. Adding the variants is its own change. The worked examples are kernels/conformance/vector_tour (e3, e4, e5, dynamic) and kernels/linear/fully_connected (e4, e5, dynamic):

  1. Store with the hardware instruction. ACTIVATE.EXACT is FP32 only, and the harness refuses it for an NX8 case. Replace each store with ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE and an activation it has (identity, relu, relu6, reciprocal, rsqrt, exp2, generic). A kernel that needs another function stays FP32: the projections store with SiLU, so they list fp32 only, and kernels/projections/test_formats.py pins that an NX8 variant is refused.
  2. Bind the QF. Every MULT and ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE names a QF half: [derived] qf = "case_qf", a CR for it in [abi], and {{ cr.qf }}.L in the program.
  3. Give the inputs a range for the type. range = { nx8 = [-4, 4] } keeps the data inside what a row's grid holds well; the harness writes each input row with its metadata.
  4. Add the variants and their tier. Add them to [kernel] formats and name the tier in [golden] tolerance (nx8 = "NX8_STEP"), then run every case: bazel run //kernels/linear/fully_connected -- --case default --format all prints each output's largest error. Record what you measured beside the tier.

docs.title: When the kernel needs more
docs.text: The kernel needs Use An input or output in a layout other than row-major, such as channel-major data or packed weights A pack transform: pack = "<name>" on the tensor, defined in the kernel folder's pack.py (one kernel's), the family folder's kernels/<family>/pack.py (shared by the family's kernels), or the shared ipu_kernels.pack (every family's). A family's transforms go in kernels/<family>/pack.py. Only when other Python imports names from them does the family put them in ipu_kernels.<family>.pack instead: the harness loads a folder's .py files by path, so one cannot import another (softmax's scratch.py imports partition_size). A test the generated cases cannot express, such as a property over many runs A test_*.py in the folder. bazel test runs it too, with the fixtures kernel, cases and run_case. Several programs that run one after another on the same XMEM A stages hook: [kernel] stages = "stages.py:run". The same program at other shapes A variant: a registry.toml entry of four lines, not a new folder. A region only some cases have, or a region placed before another when = "<bool param>" on the tensor (or "not <bool param>", or terms joined by and and or, and binding tighter), or after = "<tensor>".

docs.title: Kernels
docs.text:
A kernel is one assembly program and its declaration: an .asm file, a kernel.toml that names its parameters, XMEM regions, cases and the computations it handles, and an optional reference.py for the expected results (ADR 0006). ipu_harness lays out XMEM, runs it and checks the results.

This section covers what exists, how the emulator knows what exists, and how to add more.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text: Page What it answers Softmax Which softmax kernels exist, which shape each handles, and what they cost Convolutions Which conv2d / CHW residual_add kernels exist, which shape each handles, and what they cost Linear layers Matmul and multi-stream projection kernels for MobileViT-S's transformer blocks Normalization and shaping LayerNorm, residual add, and spatial unfold / fold / concat kernels Attention The two non-interchangeable QKᵀ / attn·V mappings and their twelve kernels MobileViT-S Kernels per MobileViT-S transformer layer, and chaining rules Kernel coverage How a computation resolves to a kernel, and every registered kernel (generated) Write a kernel How to contribute a kernel

docs.title: Finding a kernel for a computation
docs.text:
Rather than reading each kernel's docstring, ask the registry. It answers from the kernels themselves, so it cannot drift out of date:

bazel run //kernels:query -- softmax rows=32 n=300 dim=1
bazel run //kernels:query                                            # the coverage report

from ipu_harness.registry import default_registry

registry = default_registry()

# PyTorch-native: the layer plus the shape it will receive
registry.from_layer(nn.Softmax(dim=1), (32, 300))

# framework-free
registry.resolve("softmax", rows=32, n=300, dim=1)

Both return a verdict carrying the kernel, its parameters and why that kernel was chosen — or, when nothing covers the query, what each candidate objected to. Every family is a folder of kernels/; the coverage page lists them.

docs.title: Currently registered
docs.text:
Kernel coverage lists every operation and its kernels, generated from the registry when the docs are built. bazel run //kernels:query prints the same list.

Write a kernel shows the structure of a kernel under kernels/.

docs.title: Two mappings
docs.text:
Two ways to compute the same attention, differing in which operand owns a whole XMEM row:

  • query-major: qk_scores → attn_v (scores summed via ACC.ADD, attn·V summed via AGG.SUM.FIRST's float64 left-fold)
  • key-major: attn_scores_km → attn_v_bcast (scores stored key-major, attn·V summed via a single continuous float32 ACC.ADD fold, no AGG)

The two round differently (bit-different output). Feeding one chain's scores into the other chain's attn·V silently produces wrong numbers, so each stage of each chain is its own op, and the registry never hands one chain's scores to the other's consumer.

All twelve kernels are folders under kernels/attention/, run and tested as //kernels/attention/<kernel>. Each is held to a matmul reference and, bit for bit, to its datapath mirror (ipu_kernels.reference.datapath: acc_fold for the score kernels and attn_v_bcast, agg_fold for attn_v; kernels/attention/test_datapath.py). kernels/attention/test_seams.py runs each chain on one Chain: every head's score step writes its rows straight into that head's block of the attn·V kernel's P, which reads them in place.

docs.title: qk_scores
docs.text:
S[i, s] = sum_c Q[c, i] * K[c, s]

stored query-major: one whole row per query token. qk_scores_64x48 covers all 16 (stream, head) pairs per call; qk_scores_256x36 and qk_scores_16x60 score one head per call.

Kernel n_tok d (head_dim) qk_scores_16x60 16 60 qk_scores_64x48 64 48 qk_scores_256x36 256 36

docs.title: attn_scores_km
docs.text:
Same mathematical scores as qk_scores, stored key-major: one whole row per key token. Each call scores one head: its inputs are that head's Q and K. The head parameter (0–3, default 0) names which of the 4 a case generates.

Kernel n_tok d (head_dim) attn_scores_km_16x60 16 60 attn_scores_km_64x48 64 48 attn_scores_km_256x36 256 36

docs.title: attn_v
docs.text:
O[h, t, i] = sum_s P[h, i, s] * V[h, t, s]

P (input b) staged query-major (one row per query, all keys), V (input a) staged channel-major (one row per (head, channel)); O (output y) is channel-major, one row per (head, channel). Reduces via AGG.SUM.FIRST, and at n_tok = 256 adds the second 128-key chunk with AGG.SUM.

Kernel n_tok d (head_dim) attn_v_16x60 16 60 attn_v_64x48 64 48 attn_v_256x36 256 36

docs.title: attn_v_bcast
docs.text:
Same output as attn_v, summed with per-lane ACC.ADD instead of AGG. P (input b) is staged key-major (one row per key, all queries) — the transpose of attn_v's P layout, under the same name. Query by d, optionally with n_tok.

Kernel d (head_dim) n_tok (fixed) attn_v_bcast_36 36 256 attn_v_bcast_48 48 64 attn_v_bcast_60 60 16

docs.title: Queries
docs.text:
bazel run //kernels:query -- qk_scores n_tok=64 d=48
bazel run //kernels:query -- attn_scores_km n_tok=64 d=48 head=2
bazel run //kernels:query -- attn_v n_tok=64 d=48
bazel run //kernels:query -- attn_v_bcast d=48

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
The width tables below are for has_bias=False, apply_relu=False. Over the same ranges, each (has_bias, apply_relu) combination routes to one entry of kernels/convolutions/registry.toml (conv_universal, pointwise_conv_unified and depthwise_conv_universal only; the other kernels take one combination):

has_bias apply_relu 3x3 (groups=1) Pointwise (1x1) Depthwise, stride 1 False False conv_universal pointwise_conv_unified depthwise_conv_universal True True conv_universal_bn_activation pointwise_conv_unified_bn_activation depthwise_conv_universal_bn_activation False True conv_universal_bn_activation (a zero bias) pointwise_conv_unified_bn_activation (a zero bias) depthwise_conv_universal_relu True False conv_universal_bias pointwise_conv_unified_bias depthwise_conv_universal_bias

The _bias entries and depthwise_conv_universal_relu are new in E07-20; before it these queries were refused.

bazel run //kernels:query -- conv2d in_channels=8 out_channels=8 \
    kernel_size=3 stride=1 padding=1 dilation=1 groups=1 \
    has_bias=false apply_relu=false height=64 width=w --sweep w=1..640

Standard conv (groups=1, kernel_size=3, stride=1), by width, height=64:

w 1..128                     conv_universal
w 129..383                   (not covered)
w = 384                      conv_universal_wide384
w 385..511                   (not covered)
w = 512                      conv_universal_wide384
w 513..639                   (not covered)
w = 640                      conv_universal_wide384

conv_universal_wide384 (//kernels/convolutions/conv_universal_wide384) takes every width that is a multiple of 128 from 384 up, with an even out_channels. Its program is rendered for each case from the case's values: cpr (column chunks a row, width / 128) and height.

conv_universal and conv_universal_bn_activation run as //kernels/convolutions:conv_universal and //kernels/convolutions:conv_universal_bn_activation, two entries of kernels/convolutions/registry.toml over one program, kernels/convolutions/conv_universal_tpl, and answer bazel run //kernels:query with the same eleven parameters, every one required. The _bn_activation entry takes apply_relu=True with or without a bias (a zero one), and conv_universal_bias (//kernels/convolutions:conv_universal_bias) takes has_bias=True, apply_relu=False.

The pointwise and depthwise variants (pointwise_conv_unified, pointwise_conv_unified_bn_activation, pointwise_conv_unified_bias, depthwise_conv_universal, depthwise_conv_universal_bn_activation, depthwise_conv_universal_bias, depthwise_conv_universal_relu) are entries of the same registry.toml over two programs, kernels/convolutions/pointwise_conv_tpl and kernels/convolutions/depthwise_conv_tpl, and run as //kernels/convolutions:<name>. pointwise_conv_unified_bn_activation takes apply_relu=True with or without a bias (a zero one); depthwise_conv_universal_bn_activation requires both the bias and ReLU, and depthwise_conv_universal_relu takes ReLU without a bias (the same program over a zero bias).

conv_first_layer covers only 3x256x256 -> 16x128x128, stride 2, bias+ReLU. It runs as //kernels/convolutions/conv_first_layer and answers bazel run //kernels:query -- conv2d ... with the same eleven parameters.

Pointwise (groups=1, kernel_size=1), by width, height=64:

w 1..128                     pointwise_conv_unified
w 129..140                   (not covered)

in_channels must be a multiple of 8, out_channels a multiple of 4.

Depthwise, stride=1 (groups=in_channels, kernel_size=3), by width, height=64:

w 1..128                     depthwise_conv_universal
w 129..140                   (not covered)

Depthwise, stride=2 (groups=in_channels, kernel_size=3), by width, height=128:

w 1..15                      (not covered)
w = 16                       depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow
w 17..31                     (not covered)
w = 32                       depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow
w 33..63                     (not covered)
w = 64                       depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow
w 65..127                    (not covered)
w = 128                      depthwise_conv_stride2_128
w 129..140                   (not covered)

Depthwise, stride=2, width=16, by height:

h 1..15                      (not covered)
h = 16                       depthwise_conv_stride2_16
h 17..31                     (not covered)
h = 32                       depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow
h 33..63                     (not covered)
h = 64                       depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow

At width 16 depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow needs a height that is a multiple of 32. The old kernel registry (before E07) also answered it for heights 4 and 36, which its kernel then refused to build.

kernel_size is 1 or 3, groups is 1 or in_channels, dilation is 1.

docs.title: Tiled kernels
docs.text:
conv1x1, conv3x3_relu and conv3x3_relu_cin1 (//kernels/convolutions/<name>) take their own query vocabulary: in_channels, height, width, out_channels, kernel_size, stride, padding and activation, every one required. A universal query (it names dilation, groups, has_bias and apply_relu) never reaches them, and theirs never reaches a universal kernel.

bazel run //kernels:query -- conv2d in_channels=1 height=64 width=64 \
    out_channels=64 kernel_size=3 stride=1 padding=1 activation=relu
Kernel kernel_size padding activation Note conv1x1 1 0 none bias added, no ReLU conv3x3_relu 3 1 relu conv3x3_relu_cin1 3 1 relu in_channels = 1 only; preferred there (cost 0 against 1)

Each takes x ([in_channels, height, width]), w ([out_channels, in_channels, k, k]) and b ([out_channels]), and writes y ([out_channels, height, width]), all FP32. The program's tiled layout (one row per channel, padded row and column tile; the 3x3 kernels' tiles carry a one-column halo) is the family's pack transforms (kernels/convolutions/pack.py).

docs.title: Stride-2 depthwise
docs.text: depthwise_conv_stride2_narrow, depthwise_conv_stride2_128 and depthwise_conv_stride2_16 (//kernels/convolutions/<name>) run two programs on one machine state (each kernel's stages.py). Stage 1 runs depthwise_conv_tpl's program (the plain depthwise_conv_universal one) at full resolution into a scratch region; stage 2, the kernel's own program, decimates it with ACC.STRIDE into the output out. The run's cycles are the two stages' sum, and --debug stops in both. depthwise_conv_stride2_16 packs two channels per output chunk. None takes a bias or ReLU.

docs.title: residual_add
docs.text:
Elementwise y = a + b over [channels, height, width] FP32, one channel per 128-element row: //kernels/elementwise/residual_add (E07-06). Queried by num_channels (at most 1024):

bazel run //kernels:query -- residual_add num_channels=64
bazel run //kernels/elementwise/residual_add -- --benchmark

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text: input_path / output_path: raw [channels, height, width] float32. kernel_path: [out, in / groups, k, k] float32. bias_path (bias kernels): [out_channels] float32.

docs.title: Linear layers
docs.text:
All kernels in kernels/matmul/ and kernels/projections/, and fully_connected in kernels/linear/, compute

C = act(A @ W^T)          C[m, n] = act(sum_k A[m, k] * W[n, k])

with W stored output-major ([N, K] or [N_OUT, K]): row n holds all K inputs feeding output n. act is silu for the FFN1 kernels and the identity for every other kernel.

docs.title: matmul
docs.text:
Kernel M K N activation matmul_128x128 128 128 128 none matmul_128x64x128 128 64 128 none matmul_128x64x64 128 64 64 none matmul_64x64x64 64 64 64 none matmul_144x144_x128 256 144 144 none matmul_144x288_x128 256 288 144 none matmul_288x144_x128 256 144 288 silu matmul_432x144_x128 256 144 432 none matmul_192x192_x128 64 192 192 none matmul_192x384_x128 64 384 192 none matmul_384x192_x128 64 192 384 silu matmul_576x192_x128 64 192 576 none matmul_240x240_x128 16 240 240 none matmul_240x480_x128 16 480 240 none matmul_480x240_x128 16 240 480 silu matmul_720x240_x128 16 240 720 none

All 16 are entries of kernels/matmul/registry.toml over 7 templates, each run as //kernels/matmul:<kernel>: matmul_small (the four row-major kernels, one program), and for the _x128 kernels one template per distinct program: matmul_x128_2tg_c2 (144x144, 432x144, 288x144), matmul_x128_2tg_c3 (144x288), matmul_x128_c2 (192x192, 240x240, 720x240, 384x192, 480x240), matmul_x128_c2_qkv (576x192), matmul_x128_c3 (192x384) and matmul_x128_c4 (240x480). A template's activation parameter renders the store's ACTIVATE.EXACT (SiLU is not in the hardware list, so the matmuls run in FP32), and an FFN1 kernel shares its template's program.

Query: bazel run //kernels:query -- matmul m=M k=K n=N [activation=silu]. A plain query at an FFN1 shape is refused: the activation is part of the query.

docs.title: projection
docs.text:
The single-stream matmul_*_x128 shapes run over all 4 pixel streams in one invocation, against one shared weight matrix. The 12 kernels are entries of kernels/projections/registry.toml over three templates: proj_p4 (one token group, the activation a parameter), proj_p4_2tg and proj_p4_2tg_silu (two token groups). Each runs as //kernels/projections:<kernel>. The family also holds the four packed linears (op = "packed_linear"), which run on the MobileViT packed layout: see Normalization and shaping.

Kernel K N_OUT activation proj_qkv_144_p4 144 432 none proj_outproj_144_p4 144 144 none proj_ffn1_144_p4 144 288 silu proj_ffn2_144_p4 288 144 none proj_qkv_192_p4 192 576 none proj_outproj_192_p4 192 192 none proj_ffn1_192_p4 192 384 silu proj_ffn2_192_p4 384 192 none proj_qkv_240_p4 240 720 none proj_outproj_240_p4 240 240 none proj_ffn1_240_p4 240 480 silu proj_ffn2_240_p4 480 240 none

Query: bazel run //kernels:query -- projection k=K n_out=N_OUT [activation=silu]. A query that leaves activation out means activation=none: it finds the QKV, OutProj and FFN2 kernels, and an FFN1 kernel is found only with activation=silu.

docs.title: fully_connected
docs.text:
One kernel, kernels/linear/fully_connected, run and tested as //kernels/linear/fully_connected. It computes y[s, :] = w @ x[s, :] for a fixed shape: 10 samples of 128 inputs, 64 outputs, with no activation. It runs in NX8, the hardware mode, in three NX8 types with one program: e4, e5 and dynamic (ADR 0007). It accumulates in FP32, and ACTIVATE.QUANTIZE identity stores each sample's outputs as one NX8 row with its metadata, quantized to the case's QF. The case data are seeded, generated per variant inside each input's range; extremes puts every element at a range end and every_code uses every code of a row's grid. The goldens come from the shared linear op (y = linear(w, x.T).T), quantized row by row as the store quantizes, and are compared at NX8_STEP: the kernel's order of the 128-term sum can move an output across a rounding edge of its row's grid.

Query: bazel run //kernels:query -- fully_connected. The shape parameters samples, in_features and out_features each take one value (10, 128, 64).

docs.title: Data layout
docs.text:
matmul_* kernels declare their tensors in kernel.toml in one of two layouts:

  • row-major (matmul_64x64x64, matmul_128x*): a, A (M, K), and b, Wᵀ (K, N), one XMEM row per matrix row each, and the output y, C (M, N); the reference is the shared matmul op, a @ b.
  • channel-major (matmul_*_x128): b, the data D = Aᵀ as the transformer blocks hold it, (N_TG, K, N_TOK) (channel_major: one row per channel and token group), a, the weights W [N, K] output-major (output_major_weights), and y (N_TG, N, N_TOK), one row per output channel and group, the first N_TOK lanes valid. M = N_TG * N_TOK: two groups of 128 tokens at L3, one group of 64 or 16 at L4/L5. The reference is the shared linear op, activation(a @ b), as for the projections.

A proj_*_p4 kernel declares its tensors in kernel.toml, and the harness places and packs them. b holds the 4 streams' data, (N_STREAM, N_TG, K, N_TOK) (each stream's block channel-major). a holds the shared weights, [N_OUT, K], output-major. The output y is (N_STREAM, N_TG, N_OUT, N_TOK), stored as one XMEM row of 128 lanes per output channel, with the first N_TOK lanes valid. L3 (144) has N_TG = 2 token groups of 128; L4/L5 have N_TG = 1 (64 / 16 tokens padded to 128 lanes). The reference is the shared linear op, activation(a @ b).

fully_connected declares its tensors in kernel.toml too. x is [10, 128], one XMEM row per sample. w is [64, 128], output-major; its transposed pack (kernels/linear/pack.py) stores one row per input feature, holding that input's weight for each of the 64 outputs. y is [10, 64], one stored NX8 row per sample (64 lanes valid).
